entries.body:
Editable educational chapters that sit above generated notes, symbols, source entries, and asset manifests.
## Deferred Body
This entry is 14,230 markdown characters, so the app keeps a compact stub in the startup catalog and loads the full body only when requested.
## In This Entry
- Chapter Scopes
- Chapters
- Learning Paths
## Preview
Narrative chapters are the human-readable layer of the encyclopedia. They are maintained in `encyclopedia/content/narrative-chapters.json` and enriched with live upstream evidence during content generation.

## Chapter Scopes
- `Release policy`: 3
- `ROM knowledge`: 35
- `Editor guidance`: 4
- `Local generated evidence`: 1
- `Project tooling`: 1

## Chapters
- [[chapter-public-status-truthfulness|Public Status Truthfulness]] - Release policy; How to read the project status honestly: scaffold closure, semantic confidence, known limits, and what should not be overclaimed.
- [[chapter-c3-script-semantics|C3 Script Semantics]] - ROM knowledge; How C3 event/actionscript evidence is organized, what is known about opcode behavior, and where callback contracts remain active work.
- [[chapter-c3-callback-contracts|C3 Callback Contracts]] - ROM knowledge; How C3 event/actionscript bytecode crosses into native runtime helpers and long-lived installed callbacks.
- [[chapter-c3-callback-argument-semantics|C3 Callback Argument Semantics]] - ROM knowledge; How inline callroutine arguments, callback installers, and literal value names should be promoted without laundering guesses into C3 scripts.
- [[chapter-c3-movement-value-semantics|C3 Movement Value Semantics]] - ROM knowledge; How movement presets, vectors, timers, bounds, and staged movement parameters turn C3 script bytes into entity motion.
- [[chapter-c3-direction-facing-values|C3 Direction And Facing Values]] - ROM knowledge; How C3 scripts, C0 movement helpers, and C4 octant normalizers interpret direction classes, facing buckets, and sprite refresh decisions.
- [[chapter-c3-animation-template-semantics|C3 Animation And Temporary Actor Templates]] - ROM knowledge; How animation IDs, V0/V4 gates, temporary actors, wandering loops, release tails, and source-pilot templates should be read.
- [[chapter-c3-source-emission-model|C3 Source Emission Model]] - ROM knowledge; The bridge from decoded C3 script/data evidence to source-ready assembly modules and byte-equivalent rebuilds.
- [[chapter-text-vm-localization-semantics|Text VM And Localization Semantics]] - ROM knowledge; The text-command VM, recovered localization authoring syntax, macro lowering, and how text banks should be edited safely.
- [[chapter-text-command-family-model|Text Command Family Model]] - ROM knowledge; How top-level text commands, structured subcommand families, and parser-only pseudo-opcodes should be read.

entries.title: Project Overview
entries.summary: A distilled orientation for the current EarthBound decomp knowledge base.
entries.body:
The repository is structurally closed across all configured banks from `C0` through `EF`: every bank has a checked-in byte-equivalent source scaffold, and the audited source-heavy banks have no preserved native-source corridors left.

This encyclopedia should treat that as a strong foundation, not as a claim that every routine and payload is semantically finished. The useful distinction is [[terminology|terminology]]: scaffold-backed bytes, decoded source, and semantically understood systems are separate milestones.

## What This App Is For
- Present durable conclusions instead of raw note dumps.
- Link every bank, command, routine, table, and workflow to its own entry when one exists.
- Keep evidence visible through source and note references.
- Make search fast enough that it becomes the default way to move around the decomp.
- Label project-authored content separately from generated local or ROM-derived local artifacts.

## Current Reading Path
- Start with [[learning-path-index|Learning Path Index]] when you want guided reading routes through chapters, evidence notes, and practical references.
- Use [[narrative-index|Narrative Chapter Index]] for the editable educational chapters behind those routes.
- Open [[source-browser|Source Browser]] when you need the actual checked-in `.asm` file behind a bank, routine, asset, or scaffold note.
- Open [[relationship-graph|Relationship Graph]] when you want to move through connected chapters, notes, banks, routines, symbols, and assets.
- Start with [[bank-map|ROM And Bank Map]] for the whole scaffold.
- Use [[topic-index|Topic Index]] when you want distilled knowledge areas instead of raw evidence-note files.
- Check [[upstream-status|Upstream Source Status]] to confirm which decomp workspace generated this encyclopedia build.
- Check [[catalog-build-status|Catalog Build Status]] to see build mode, provenance counts, and release readiness signals.
- Check [[rom-status|ROM And Generated Content Status]] before running ROM-backed extraction or validation.
- Check [[release-artifact-policy|Release Artifact Policy]] before deciding whether a generated output belongs in a distributable build.
- Use [[runtime-systems|Runtime Systems]] for C0/C1/C2/C4/EF source-heavy work.
- Use [[script-and-text-vms|Script And Text VMs]] for C3 event/actionscript and text-command semantics.
- Use [[asset-contracts|Assets And Data Contracts]] for graphics, map, audio, and generated table banks.

entries.body:
Readable source-bank closure is complete for the audited runtime banks. The remaining work is semantic polish: names, comments, data contracts, side-effect documentation, and validation paths.

## Priority Runtime Banks
- [[bank-c0|C0]]: overworld, entity, task, movement, interaction, collision, teleport, and PPU helper contracts.
- [[bank-c1|C1]]: text engine, CCS leaves, menus, battle front ends, and file select.
- [[bank-c2|C2]]: battle runtime, action dispatch, target selection, status/effect families, and battle visuals.
- [[bank-c4|C4]]: renderer-facing text tile staging, movement presentation, window/color HDMA, file select, town map, and presentation effects.
- [[bank-ef|EF]]: save/SRAM, debug/menu routines, map tables, text/help script runs, glyph masks, and late tail data.

entries.title: Terminology
entries.summary: The key completion terms used throughout the decomp.
entries.body:
## Scaffold-backed
Bytes are represented in checked-in assembler artifacts and pass byte-equivalence validation.

## Decoded Source
Bytes have been converted into instruction-by-instruction assembly, table definitions, or typed data emitters.

## Semantically Understood
Decoded source has reliable names, comments, call/data evidence, side-effect contracts, and editing constraints.

The project is scaffold-backed ROM-wide. The next encyclopedia job is to make the semantic layer navigable.

items.title: Asset And Data Contracts
items.summary: How graphics, UI, map, battle visual, audio, and table payloads are represented as source-safe contracts.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Contract Model
concepts.summary: An asset/data contract is the evidence-backed boundary between original ROM bytes and editor or port work. It does not contain the copyrighted payload. It records what owns the bytes, how those bytes are located, what decoder or renderer shape is expected, and how a local user can regenerate or verify the derived output from their own ROM. That makes contracts different from raw extraction. A raw `.gfx`, `.pal`, `.arr`, BRR sample, collision table, or object bundle can be extracted locally, but the checked-in source-safe object is the recipe: stable ID, bank/range, size, hash, decoder class, dependencies, uncertainty, and validation command. Those recipes are the durable knowledge layer.

concepts.title: The Four Layers
concepts.summary: ROM recipe layer: records the source span, expected byte count, expected SHA-1, compression, and table or pointer evidence. Portable asset layer: describes ignored local outputs such as raw slices, decompressed bytes, preview PNGs, palette JSON, object bundles, scene contracts, or audio intermediates. Semantic ID layer: gives tools stable names such as battle background IDs, sprite group IDs, map object IDs, map tileset IDs, and table-contract names so consumers do not depend on bare SNES addresses. Validation layer: proves the recipe against a user-supplied ROM and records which generated reports or hashes make the contract reproducible.

concepts.title: Current Coverage
concepts.summary: The manifest pipeline now covers every currently mapped asset/data bank from `CA` through `EE`, plus the hand-curated EF debug seed manifest. The latest local status reports `38` manifests, `2218` assets, and `6174` output recipes. The output recipes include raw ROM-backed outputs, LZHAL decompression, palette JSON and swatches, battle-background previews, battle-sprite previews, default-palette overworld sprite sheets, and composed battle-background and battle-sprite PNGs. This does not make every asset family semantically final. It gives the project a repeatable source-safe inventory. Interpretation remains a separate layer: which assets belong together, which runtime tables choose them, what renderer assumptions are proven, and which editor fields have evidence.

concepts.title: Major Families
concepts.summary: `CA..CE`: battle backgrounds, battle sprites, palettes, arrangements, animation visuals, and related compressed graphics. `D1..D5`: overworld sprite payloads, later joined through sprite group, frame, animation-role, map placement, and object bundle contracts. `CF..D0`, `D5`, `D8`, `DA`, `DE`, `DF`, and `EF`: map doors, placements, battle/menu tables, collision records, map palettes, tile animation graphics, upload scripts, and pointer tables. `E0..E1`: UI, font, town map, intro/title/ending/cast, and presentation assets. `E2..EE`: audio-pack payloads, now promoted from bank-level coverage into `LOAD_SPC700_DATA` stream contracts, track-to-pack snapshot rules, and a renderer/backend boundary.

concepts.title: Editing Rules
concepts.summary: The safe editing unit is the highest contract that already preserves the dependency chain. For a single compressed battle-background graphic, the useful edit boundary includes its graphics payload, matching palette, arrangement, preview renderer, and manifest hash. For an overworld NPC, the useful edit boundary is not just a D1-D5 `.gfx` payload; it includes sprite group identity, runtime slot records, animation role, map placement, movement/script target, event flag, and text pointer context. A generated preview is evidence that a decoder path is plausible. It is not by itself an authoring schema. A family reaches editable status only when the contract explains stable fields, runtime-selected values, and which local outputs are disposable rebuild products. Keep ROM-derived payloads in ignored build/cache paths. Commit manifests, tools, contracts, summaries, and validation reports only when they are payload-free. Use semantic IDs in editor and port work; keep raw bank addresses as provenance and compatibility anchors. Treat palette, arrangement, collision, OAM, and script dependencies as part of an asset's contract when the runtime consumes them together. Do not rename a generated asset family as semantically final until the relevant runtime selector or table has been followed.

concepts.title: Confidence Boundary
concepts.summary: The current asset pipeline is strong at inventory, extraction, and many visual preview paths. It is strongest where runtime contracts have been joined: map objects, sprite roles, collision pointer/runtime bits, palette pointer tables, tile animation upload records, and many battle visual assets. The main weak spots are the places where a payload is mapped but the consumer-side authoring meaning is still thin: some map collision low bits, DA palette metadata words, text/common palette preview joining, palette-settings-only tilesets, event/actionscript behavior semantics, and the distinction between ROM audio facts and local playback/export tooling. Those limits belong in the visible contract layer rather than hidden in generated pages.

items.summary: ROM-facing audio-pack facts: bank coverage, loader stream shape, track-to-pack recipes, and local regeneration rules.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Current Boundary
concepts.summary: The audio banks now have a payload-free contract layer for `169` audio packs, `192` music tracks, and `169` pack pointer entries. Every represented pack parses as an `ok` `LOAD_SPC700_DATA` stream, and the track table resolves to the primary, secondary, and sequence pack order used by `CHANGE_MUSIC`. The ROM-facing facts are the source ranges, byte counts, SHA-1 hashes, stream block transcripts, pack selector evidence, and track mappings. ROM-derived payload bytes, APU RAM images, SPC snapshots, and WAV renders are generated locally from a user's ROM and stay out of the checked-in encyclopedia.

concepts.title: What Is Now Teachable
concepts.summary: Banks `E2..EE` are overwhelmingly source-order audio-pack payloads, with E6's custom `AUDIO_PACK_1` handled as a special inline block instead of being double-counted. Audio packs are modeled as loader streams, not opaque blobs: each stream has one or more destination blocks and a terminating loader handshake. Music tracks can be described as pack recipes: primary sample pack, secondary sample pack, and sequence pack, with unchanged or `$FF` entries skipped by the runtime. The local corpus tooling can rebuild deterministic APU RAM and later SPC/WAV evidence for selected tracks, but those outputs are local ROM-derived artifacts rather than checked-in ROM documentation. Generated audio outputs belong under ignored `build/audio` paths. The committed encyclopedia contains contracts, not mirrored audio payload bytes.

concepts.title: ROM And Tooling Boundary
concepts.summary: The pack contracts describe the ROM's loadable music payloads. Backend work describes how our tools replay those payloads through emulation, capture state, and render WAVs. Keep those layers separate when reading the encyclopedia: `LOAD_SPC700_DATA`, pack pointers, track recipes, and `CHANGE_MUSIC` behavior are ROM knowledge; ares harnesses, libgme renders, result summaries, and playback/export manifests are project tooling evidence.

items.title: Audio Pack Stream Contracts
items.summary: How audio packs are represented as `LOAD_SPC700_DATA` streams with source ranges, block transcripts, parse status, and validation hashes.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Stream Model
concepts.summary: The runtime owner for this contract is `C0:AB06 LoadSpc700DataStream`. The loader waits for the SPC ready signature on the APU ports, temporarily disables NMI while it streams data, writes block payloads to APU destinations, and exits through the loader's final handshake. The portable contract is intentionally simpler than the SNES routine. Each audio pack is represented as a sequence of blocks: a `u16 payload_byte_count`, then a `u16 apu_destination` plus payload bytes when the count is nonzero. A zero count terminates the stream and records the `$0500` terminal handshake behavior.

concepts.title: Coverage
concepts.summary: `169` audio packs are represented. `169` pack pointer entries are represented. All represented streams currently parse with status `ok`. Every known audio pack has a byte-exact ROM source range and SHA-1. The track table currently has `0` unused pack IDs. E6's custom `AUDIO_PACK_1` block is represented as a custom inline audio pack instead of a normal source-order insert.

concepts.title: Bank Run Boundary
concepts.summary: The source-order run covers the heavy `E2..EE` audio banks, with the large `EE:9201..EE:FFFF` tail still called out as a separate unexplained slack region. The bank maps prove source readiness for the opaque payloads, while this stream contract proves that the payloads can be replayed through the same loader shape the game uses. Pack identity is not the same thing as internal audio meaning. The pack contract says where bytes come from, how they load, how they validate, and which tracks select them. BRR sample names, sequence commands, and instrument semantics need their own evidence before they become ROM-facing facts.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: The safe stream-editing unit is a complete pack transcript. Changing a payload byte, destination, or block count without updating range/hash validation and track ownership desynchronizes the loader contract from the source ROM evidence. Audio packs are validated load streams at this layer. Sample and sequence authoring is a later layer that consumes this contract instead of replacing it.

entries.summary: Guided reading route for Audio SPC Renderer Boundary.

steps.title: Start With The Narrative
steps.summary: Read the chapter first so the evidence has context and confidence boundaries.

items.title: Audio SPC Renderer Boundary
items.summary: Where ROM audio state ends and local playback/export evidence begins: APU RAM seeds, SPC snapshots, WAV renders, and runtime-state requirements.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: What The Seed Contains
concepts.summary: The APU RAM seed contains the 64 KiB memory image after the relevant `LOAD_SPC700_DATA` streams have been applied in runtime order. It proves that the pack stream contracts and track mapping can construct deterministic memory images. A seed is not a running SPC state. It records loaded memory and the post-load track-command requirement, but it does not by itself prove the registers, DSP state, timers, mailbox timing, or rendered audio.

concepts.title: Missing Runtime State
concepts.summary: SPC700 CPU registers are not captured. DSP registers are not captured. APU control and timer state are not captured. APUIO mailbox state is only partially modeled. Driver elapsed cycles and post-command timing are not captured.

concepts.title: Renderer Gates
concepts.summary: `diagnostic_apu_ram_seed` is open and useful today. `complete_spc_snapshot` requires runtime state capture or emulation evidence. `local_pcm_wav_export` is tooling evidence: it requires a renderer backend, output hashes, and render metrics. `snes_spc` is a lightweight renderer lane once a suitable SPC snapshot exists. `ares` is the accuracy-first lane for proving command delivery, runtime state, and capture timing.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A built APU RAM image is loaded-memory evidence. A playable/exportable artifact also needs a runtime-state source, backend identity, timing basis, output hashes, and render metrics. A renderer entry must identify whether it is describing ROM behavior or project tooling. Registers, DSP state, timers, command byte, timing basis, and backend version are tooling evidence unless they are tied directly back to ROM execution.

items.summary: How music tracks resolve to pack load order and diagnostic 64 KiB APU RAM seeds without claiming complete SPC playback state.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Track Load Order
concepts.summary: `CHANGE_MUSIC` gives the snapshot contract its order. A track resolves to primary sample pack, secondary sample pack, and sequence pack. The runtime loads changed packs in that order, skips unchanged entries, skips `$FF`, updates `CURRENT_MUSIC_TRACK`, and finally writes the one-based track index to `APUPort0` through `C0:ABBD`. Cold start adds one more rule: `C4:FB58 InitializeMusicSubsystem` loads the row-0 sequence/common pack before ordinary track changes. A snapshot builder that omits that bootstrap can still load pack bytes, but it is not modeling the same runtime state.

concepts.title: Diagnostic APU RAM Seed
concepts.summary: The snapshot corpus can construct a 64 KiB APU RAM image after replaying the selected pack streams. The seed is ROM-derived and must remain an ignored local diagnostic artifact. The seed records the post-load track command requirement, but it does not execute the APU driver after writing the command byte. Renderer fixtures should point to ignored seed files and pack transcripts instead of embedding ROM-derived bytes in committed JSON. The useful status label for this stage is `diagnostic_apu_ram_seed`, not `complete_spc_snapshot`.

concepts.title: Tooling Contract
concepts.summary: The generated tooling path has distinct jobs: build and validate audio pack contracts, inspect track-to-pack mappings, build selected track snapshots, build an ignored corpus, and create renderer fixtures. Those jobs are not the renderer. Track snapshot entries describe which packs a track uses and what memory image can be reconstructed. Playback and export evidence belongs to the backend/tooling layer.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A track edit starts as a change to the track's pack recipe. Changing a sequence pack, sample pack, or common bootstrap assumption requires rebuilding the snapshot corpus and comparing the pack transcript before playback/export results are trusted.

items.summary: How D5 battle actions, PSI abilities, enemy configuration rows, and battle text/action consumers fit together.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: D5 Gameplay Spine
concepts.summary: D5 now has a practical gameplay-table spine. The split plan reconciles the post-pad region exactly and identifies the source-order families that matter for battle, items, shops, teleport, phone, growth, map destinations, timed delivery, initial stats, and enemies. For battle editing, three D5 families are the current anchors: the battle action descriptor table at `D5:7B68`, the battle PSI ability table at `D5:8A50`, and the enemy configuration table at `D5:9589`.

concepts.title: Action Rows
concepts.summary: The `D5:7B68` action table is no longer merely battle-action-like. The strongest current read is a 12-byte row: direction, target, action type, PP or cost byte, message pointer, and action handler pointer. Early entries line up cleanly with no-effect, bash, shoot, spy, pray, and the PSI quartet runs. The confidence is strongest where table metadata, reference layout, local wrapper quartets, shared helper signatures, and C2 action bodies all agree. Later rows now have status, stat/resource, physical/special, and flavor-tail anchors, but the table should still label tail outliers and reference-assisted names honestly.

concepts.title: Battle Action Confidence
concepts.summary: The early table is the cleanest slice: PSI Rockin, Fire, Freeze, and Thunder rows line up by direction, target, type, cost, message pointer, and C2 handler pointer. Later rows have improved local anchors too: status-action bodies, stat/resource mutation bodies, physical/special wrappers, and flavor-tail no-op rows. That gives the editor model a tiered confidence map. Early action rows can be presented with strong names and fields. Later rows should show their current local body evidence, but keep reference-assisted names and unresolved tail outliers visibly qualified. Strong: row stride, first four metadata bytes, message pointer, handler pointer, early PSI quartets, and several late C2 body families. Medium: reference-backed row names where local handler behavior is compatible but not fully followed end to end. Open: tail entries whose table position is clear but whose gameplay role is still presentation-heavy or caller-thin.

concepts.title: Enemy Rows
concepts.summary: `D5:9589` is the strongest current local crosswalk to the enemy configuration table. The record stride is `0x5E`, local text extraction from `D5:9589 + 1 + n * 0x5E` yields enemy names, and local code reaches the family through a selector with stride `#$005E`. The safest field names are the ones backed by both local consumers and the reference struct shape: article flag, enemy name, encounter text pointer, death text pointer, music, final action, final action argument, row, max-called behavior, and mirror success. These rows are not just stats; they connect battle presentation, text, audio, and action selection.

concepts.title: Cross Table Joins
concepts.summary: The most useful battle model is not a single table. Enemy rows can select final actions, action rows point at text and handlers, PSI ability rows point back into action rows, and C1/C2/C3 helpers turn those fields into menu choices, target prompts, row formatting, and battle text. That is the reason battle and enemy chapters should be read with the PSI/menu chapter rather than as a competing explanation. `D5:7B68`, `D5:8A50`, and `D5:9589` are separate storage families, but the runtime presents them as one battle-facing authoring surface.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A battle table edit should follow the row to its consumers before making a name stronger. If a field points at EF text, C2 action code, C1 menu text, or C3 formatting helpers, that downstream behavior is part of the contract. The table is joined data: enemy row, selected action row, action message pointer, action handler pointer, PSI ability row when applicable, and battle visual/text neighbors. Raw D5 offsets are provenance, not the primary authoring model.

steps.title: Start With The Narrative
steps.summary: Read the chapter first so the evidence has context and confidence boundaries.

items.title: Battle Visual Asset Contracts
items.summary: How battle backgrounds, battle sprites, palettes, arrangements, and C2/C3/C4 visual runtime evidence fit together.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: System Shape
concepts.summary: Battle visuals are not a single asset type. They are a family of compressed graphics, palettes, arrangements, size metadata, token tables, runtime palette effects, and renderer staging code. The source-safe contract should keep those pieces linkable even when the decoded PNG preview is only a local build artifact. The current manifest pipeline can extract and preview palette-aware battle backgrounds and battle sprites. For battle backgrounds, matching graphics, palette, and arrangement payloads can produce composed arrangement previews. For battle sprites, observed enemy-table sprite/palette combinations can produce size-aware composed previews.

concepts.title: What Is Proven
concepts.summary: `CA..CE` asset maps provide bank ownership, labels, payload filenames, CPU spans, file offsets, sizes, and first-byte fingerprints for battle visual payloads. The extraction pipeline records raw and LZHAL-decompressed outputs, palette-aware tile previews, battle-background arrangement previews, and battle-sprite composed previews. C2 notes cover battle background loading, palette effects, battle sprite rendering, and palette-tail behavior. C3 notes expose battle visual token, offset, and palette table evidence, giving the visual byte payloads runtime selector context. C4 notes cover visual frame copy and footprint tables, which matters for how visual data reaches presentation memory.

concepts.title: Authoring Boundary
concepts.summary: A battle background edit is safe only when the graphics, palette, arrangement, compression, and preview path remain coherent. A battle sprite edit also needs size and palette pairing evidence from the observed enemy table path. The editor-facing unit should be a composed contract, not a single decompressed byte stream. Generated names like `BATTLE_BACKGROUND_GFX_86` or `BATTLE_BACKGROUND_ARR_43` are stable handles for tooling, but the display-facing meaning should come from runtime use, enemy/table context, and rendered previews rather than from the numeric suffix alone.

concepts.title: Known Limits
concepts.summary: Preview coverage is strong for observed combinations, but not every possible runtime composition is necessarily a designed authoring combination. Palette effects and battle visual tokens should be described through C2/C3 runtime evidence before editor UI treats them as intuitive art controls. The manifest layer preserves payload provenance; final battle-effect semantics still need curated pages for major effect families.

steps.title: Start With The Narrative

items.title: C3 Animation And Temporary Actor Templates
items.summary: How animation IDs, V0/V4 gates, temporary actors, wandering loops, release tails, and source-pilot templates should be read.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Template Model
concepts.summary: Many C3 scripts are better read as templates than as one-off scene scripts. They install a callback, start a recurring animation task, seed a few script variables, wait on a native predicate, and then release or hand off the current visual entity. The key values in these templates are often animation IDs, `V0` or `V4` gates, wait timers, random-choice lists, target coordinates, and release-tail addresses. Their meaning depends on the template, not on a global enum.

concepts.title: Temporary Actor Family
concepts.summary: The temporary actor movement notes split several useful families: timed-delivery cleanup pulses, `C4:0015`-gated pulse-and-release loops, a `V0`-selected animation phase loop, random wandering setup, NPC attention or neighbor-cache loops, and shared current-entity release tails. For example, `C3:A3B7` clears `V4`, classifies the current slot against area bounds, chooses a cardinal direction or adjusts the current direction, installs the direction through C0 helpers, derives a movement timer, then chooses a random wait from `30,60,90,120` before looping.

concepts.title: V0 And V4
concepts.summary: `V4` is a strong local gate in movement pulse families: some loops only show animation `1` while `V4` is true, or count down before restoring animation `0`. `V0` appears as an animation phase selector in temporary actor and attention paths, where several short cases choose different pulse/wait shapes. Those are family-local meanings. `V0` and `V4` are script variables with known roles in specific templates, not universal variable names across all of C3.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A template editor should show the whole shape: installed callbacks, started tasks, animation IDs, script variables, wait timers, random lists, native predicates, and release tail. Editing just the animation byte without the task and predicate context is too narrow. Animation IDs `0`, `1`, and `FF` are common in these templates, but their authoring meaning should stay tied to the visual-profile helpers and script family that use them. Repetition alone is not enough to make a global animation enum.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Operand Boundary
concepts.summary: The C3 decoder now knows enough about callback byte shapes to be useful: it distinguishes bank-local short calls from low-word callback installers, prints named callback targets, labels common operands such as frames, script variables, animation IDs, and event-flag words, and keeps raw bytes visible on every decoded line. That is a readability layer, not a license to name every literal. Inline arguments become semantics only when the target callback, local script family, or downstream runtime helper proves what the value controls.

concepts.title: Two Argument Classes
concepts.summary: `EVENT_CALLROUTINE` arguments are consumed immediately by the native helper and usually belong to that helper's contract. Callback installer operands are different: opcodes such as `EVENT_SET_POSITION_CHANGE_CALLBACK` and `EVENT_SET_PHYSICS_CALLBACK` store low-word targets that bind long-lived C0 or C4 behavior to the active entity. The earlier decoder bug is a good warning sign. Callback installers looked like C3-local pointers until the binding correction proved they commonly point back to C0 callback routines. The durable lesson is that operand shape is not the same as operand meaning.

concepts.title: Current Strong Labels
concepts.summary: Mutation operation bytes can use the C0 interpreter names `AND`, `OR`, `ADD`, and `EOR` because the interpreter table proves them. Event flag words can be labeled where the callback argument schema already ties them to flag checks. Velocity and relative-position words can show signed decimal meaning beside raw hex values. `$5D9A` can be called a queue-pending or transient special-state flag where the C0/EF queue notes support that read. Callback pointers for movement, projection, velocity integration, passive no-op behavior, and screen-position callbacks can use their C0/C4 names once the installer opcode class is known.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A C3 editor should show raw operand bytes, friendly labels, and evidence level together. Strong labels can become controls. Medium labels should stay descriptive. Weak labels should remain literal until a local family note or native callback contract proves the field. The safest UI is not a screen full of raw hex or a screen full of overconfident names. It is a joined view: opcode, operand bytes, target helper, known argument schema, installed callback lifetime, and the notes that prove the interpretation.

items.title: C3 Callback Contracts
items.summary: How C3 event/actionscript bytecode crosses into native runtime helpers and long-lived installed callbacks.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Two Bridges
concepts.summary: C3 scripts enter native behavior through two different bridges. `EVENT_CALLROUTINE` is immediate: the VM reads inline arguments, calls a native helper, and continues with a returned condition or result. Callback installers are durable: they bind per-frame or stateful native behavior to an object slot after the current bytecode instruction is done. That is why callback notes are not optional background. They define what the script can safely express. The same opcode stream can have very different editing risk depending on whether it merely waits, calls a helper once, or installs a movement, physics, collision, presentation, or text callback that keeps owning runtime behavior.

concepts.title: Semantic Groups
concepts.summary: The current callback audit groups targets into practical editing families: current-slot state, movement, visual profile, timed delivery, overworld runtime, presentation rendering, text presentation, collision, entity spawn, neighbor cache, party-facing behavior, world-state restore, battle runtime, and intro-integrity checks. These groups are intentionally more useful than raw addresses. The editing constraint is whether a value chooses a movement pulse, controls a visual profile, tests party state, or dispatches a presentation effect. The raw bank address remains provenance; the group is the first reader-facing contract.

concepts.title: Good Enough Boundary
concepts.summary: The callback layer is good enough when generated reports are truthful and useful. It is not necessary to give every literal a perfect symbolic story before the encyclopedia can teach the system. The safer rule is to keep animation IDs, direction classes, family variables, and helper arguments literal until local evidence proves a stronger name. When a callback is only known as a native target plus observed family, the entry says exactly that. Overclaiming makes editing less safe; precise uncertainty is part of the contract.

steps.title: Start With The Narrative

items.title: C3 Direction And Facing Values
items.summary: How C3 scripts, C0 movement helpers, and C4 octant normalizers interpret direction classes, facing buckets, and sprite refresh decisions.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Direction Is Layered
concepts.summary: C3 direction values are not just north/east/south/west labels. C4 uses a 16-bit angle circle, octants of `0x2000`, rounded and floored octant helpers, alternate facing tables, sprite-facing buckets, and walk-direction encodings. C0 movement helpers then cache or compare those values while installing vectors and refreshing visual profiles. That means the same small numeric range can mean different things depending on the helper: script-facing direction mode, rounded angle octant, coarse sprite-facing quadrant, walk/step direction encoding, or player/current facing remap.

concepts.title: Proven Conversions
concepts.summary: `C4:6B0A` rounds an angle to the nearest octant and caches it in the current slot. `C4:6B2D` floors an angle to an octant. `C4:6B37` rotates an octant by half a turn. `C4:6AA3` maps octants to coarse sprite-facing buckets used to decide whether `C0:A48F` should refresh the current slot. `C4:6B51` maps rounded angles through a walk-direction table used by movement-target callers. `C4:6B65` and `C4:6B79` set current-slot targets from player or staged coordinates.

concepts.title: C3 Facing Patterns
concepts.summary: The C3 source pilots show several repeated direction/facing idioms. Facing-pulse helpers alternate visual countdown states before returning. Live-area facing scripts choose random facing-cycle steps and mix fast/slow timing with longer movement paths. Animation-port direction tasks use `V4` or animation-port state to drive direction loops. These patterns are useful because byte validation is already passing, but they are not yet all wired into the main C3 source scaffold. items.title: C3 Movement Value Semantics
items.summary: How movement presets, vectors, timers, bounds, and staged movement parameters turn C3 script bytes into entity motion.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Movement Stack
concepts.summary: C3 movement values only make sense as a stack. C3 scripts choose directions, presets, waits, tasks, and inline parameters. C0 turns direction and speed into per-slot velocity words and task timers. C4 projects angles, checks cached targets, classifies area bounds, and refreshes facing when movement crosses a coarse visual bucket. The editor-facing meaning of a movement value is therefore rarely local to C3. A literal may be a direction class, timer count, radius, target coordinate, speed-like field, or preset parameter depending on which native helper consumes it.

concepts.title: Pulse Presets
concepts.summary: The movement pulse preset family around `C3:A0B2..AB26` is one of the best C3 value-semantics anchors. The task loops alternate animation `1` and `0`, call current-slot visual refresh helpers, and vary their pauses: 24-frame, 12-frame, 9-frame, 6-frame, 2-frame, and `V4`-gated variants. The AAxx and ABxx setup helpers install those tasks after setting physics callbacks, zeroing velocities, setting animation `0`, and passing literal pairs to `C0:A685`. The byte shape is firm, while the exact field-level meaning of some `C0:A685` pairs remains intentionally literal.

concepts.title: Vectors And Timers
concepts.summary: `C0:C83B` is the movement-vector bridge. It takes a direction or mode value, uses the current slot's speed-like field, and writes signed X/Y velocity component pairs. Modes `0,2,4,6` are axial; modes `1,3,5,7` are diagonal and use a fixed-point diagonal scale. Timer helpers such as `C0:CA4E`, `C0:CBD3`, and `C0:CC11` translate active vectors, speed scale, or cached target distance into task timers. This explains the common script idiom: set direction, install vector, compute timer, wait or loop until the movement helper reports completion.

concepts.title: Bounds And Parameter Tables
concepts.summary: `C4:7225` and `C4:7269` give random-wander and area-bound scripts a concrete model: set a rectangle around the current slot, then classify the slot as inside or outside by side. C3 scripts can then choose a fresh cardinal direction or continue a wandering loop. The C3 map movement parameter table at `C3:E1D8..E240` is part of the same value family. It contains placement direction parameters, staged movement direction parameters, subtile offset sets, and door-candidate direction offsets. Some blocks have direct consumer proof; the `E1D8..E1FF` prefix still needs tighter C0-side struct names before it receives a stronger label.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A movement editor should not expose one generic `value` field for C3 scripts. It should expose the value in the context of its consumer: pulse frame count, script variable gate, movement direction mode, area-bound radius, target coordinate, subtile offset, door-probe offset, or native-helper literal. If the consumer is known but the field name is not, keep the literal visible and attach the native helper. That is still useful, and it avoids turning repeated movement bytes into false enums.

items.title: C3 Script Semantics
items.summary: How C3 event/actionscript evidence is organized, what is known about opcode behavior, and where callback contracts remain active work.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Milestone Boundary
concepts.summary: C3 is no longer best described as an unknown byte frontier. The current scaffold is byte-equivalent across the full bank, the residual range tracker is closed, and the event/actionscript byte layer has a stable first-pass semantic model. The open work has moved from finding bytes to explaining what edits mean. That distinction matters for readers. A generated C3 payload entry identifies where a script lives; the curated contract explains VM opcode shape, callback handoff, entity-slot side effects, map or battle runtime dependencies, and the confidence boundary for changing values.

concepts.title: What Is Proven
concepts.summary: The current audit covers `181` script rows. All `181` are syntactically complete, all have stable non-UNKNOWN names, and the current audit records no unknown callback, opcode, or name frontier. The callback layer is also seeded: `86` native `EVENT_CALLROUTINE` targets and `17` installed callback targets are tracked as explicit contracts. The source-pilot layer is strong enough to guide authoring work. It covers `140` event/actionscript families and validates `56518` bytes, with the source-pilot candidate frontier recorded as zero remaining candidate bytes. That does not make every literal symbolic, but it does mean the project has enough structure to write editing rules instead of just catalog entries.

concepts.title: Reader Model
concepts.summary: Script payload row: the generated entry that names the bank range, extraction class, and decode status. VM opcode: the C3 bytecode operation that advances the event/actionscript interpreter. Native callback bridge: an `EVENT_CALLROUTINE` target that consumes inline arguments and returns a condition or result to the VM. Installed callback: a tick, position, physics, or related routine that keeps acting after the current instruction finishes. Source pilot or source module: the human-readable assembly boundary that proves bytes can be emitted without changing behavior.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A safe C3 edit keeps the VM stream, callback target, inline argument shape, and downstream runtime state together. Do not rename a literal as a semantic enum just because it repeats. Promote a value only when local evidence ties it to a family, callback, runtime table, animation preset, direction class, or source-pilot validation. The useful editing unit is often larger than one payload. A movement script may depend on object-slot state, collision behavior, text presentation, and a map object record. A battle visual script may depend on C2/C4 runtime selectors and CA-CE visual assets. The entry relationship graph exposes those neighbors instead of treating the C3 byte stream as self-contained.

concepts.title: Open Work
concepts.summary: The remaining work is value semantics and source/editing rules: family-specific variables, animation IDs, direction classes, callback return meanings, and source-emission hardening. Those are refinement tasks over a closed byte layer, not blockers to writing the narrative model.

items.summary: The bridge from decoded C3 script/data evidence to source-ready assembly modules and byte-equivalent rebuilds.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Purpose
concepts.summary: C3 source emission is the step between knowing what bytes are and making them maintainable. The goal is not to dump assembly for its own sake. The goal is to carve the bank into source units whose labels, local data, external symbols, and adjacent tables can rebuild without changing bytes. The source plan currently tracks `6` modules and `26` source units. All queued units are source-ready, all prototype modules are present, and the remaining work is build-candidate hardening: assembler syntax, external symbol naming, byte matching, and preserving adjacent visual/script data as data rather than accidental code.

concepts.title: Module Shape
concepts.summary: `src/c3/window_text_helpers.asm` covers window and text helper code around `C3:E450..C3:E84E`. `src/c3/inventory_equipment_tracked_items.asm` covers inventory, equipment, and tracked-item helpers around `C3:E977..C3:EC1F`. `src/c3/hp_pp_adjustment_helpers.asm` covers HP/PP adjustment helpers around `C3:EC1F..C3:EE14`. `src/c3/equipment_battle_selector_helpers.asm` covers equipment and battle selector helpers around `C3:EE14..C3:EF23`. `src/c3/jeff_repair_psi_helpers.asm` covers Jeff repair and PSI helper code around `C3:F1EC..C3:F2B1`. `src/c3/battle_visual_effect_helpers.asm` covers battle visual effect helpers around `C3:F5F9..C3:FB1F`.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: Promote C3 source in pieces that preserve their byte neighbors. Script tables, visual tables, callback argument data, and helper routines often touch the same conceptual feature but cannot always share the same source unit. The emission plan keeps those boundaries explicit so edits do not accidentally turn data into code or code into a guessed table. A C3 source unit is ready to teach when it has a named range, a reason for the boundary, validation evidence, and a statement about what remains literal. It is ready to edit only when assembler output, symbol dependencies, and adjacent data ownership are all stable.

entries.title: D5 Battle Action Field Families Learning Path
entries.summary: Guided reading route for D5 Battle Action Field Families.

steps.title: Start With The Narrative
steps.summary: Read the chapter first so the evidence has context and confidence boundaries.

items.title: D5 Battle Action Field Families
items.summary: How late battle action rows split into numeric effects, physical/special wrappers, status writers, PSI links, and flavor-only tails.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Row Contract
concepts.summary: `D5:7B68` is the battle action descriptor table. The strongest current row model is `12` bytes: direction, target, action type, PP or cost byte, message pointer, and action handler pointer. The first four bytes are metadata. The first pointer is battle text or presentation. The second pointer is live C2 action behavior consumed by the battle action dispatch path. Most useful field-family work happens by following that second pointer.

concepts.title: Strong Families
concepts.summary: Early PSI quartets: Rockin, Fire, Freeze, and Thunder rows line up by action metadata, cost progression, shared message pointer, and wrapper/helper families. Concentration or PSI-seal writers: `C2:8D5A` and `C2:A3D1` both write battler affliction byte `+0x21 = 4` and display the same success/failure text family. Stat/resource mutators: `C2:8E42`, `C2:8EAE`, `C2:8F21`, `C2:9E38`, and `C2:9E7F` mutate PP, guts, offense, or defense and display amount-bearing messages. Physical/special late actions: `C2:8F97` is a poison-on-hit physical action, `C2:8FF9` is a double-bash wrapper, and `C2:900B` is a fire-damage or flaming-fireball wrapper. Flavor tails: `C2:9033` and neighboring no-op tails carry little or no gameplay behavior; their visible effect is mostly message-side or upstream controller-side.

concepts.title: Confidence Map
concepts.summary: Some rows are strong enough for editor-facing names. `C2:8FF9` is an exact double-bash wrapper over the anchored bash family. `C2:8F21` is a paired offense/defense reducer with direct battler-field mutation. `C2:9033` is best taught as a flavor-only no-op tail rather than unresolved mechanics. Other rows should remain strongest-fit names. `C2:8E42` is clearly PP-reduction or PP-sapping, but the final symbolic export name still depends partly on field naming and reference crosswalk. `C2:900B` is clearly fire-damage-like, but the target byte `+0x3A` remains a field-level follow-up.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A battle action row should be edited as metadata plus behavior: direction, target, type, cost, message pointer, and C2 handler pointer. Changing the handler without its message pointer can make the table lie to the player; changing the metadata without the handler can make targeting or PP behavior lie to the runtime. For flavor-only rows, the correct editor control may be text selection rather than mechanics. No-op handlers are not necessarily unknown; sometimes they are the contract.

items.title: D5 Character Growth Table Contracts
items.summary: How EXP thresholds, stat growth variables, initial stats, level-up helpers, and statistic selectors fit into the character-growth contract.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Storage Families
concepts.summary: D5 has three character-growth support tables that now have exact spans. `EXP_TABLE` lives at `D5:8F49..D5:9588`, has `4` rows, and uses stride `0x190`. `STATS_GROWTH_VARS` lives at `D5:EA5B..D5:EA76`, has `4` rows, and uses stride `0x07`. `INITIAL_STATS` lives at `D5:F5F5..D5:F648`, has `4` rows, and uses stride `0x15`. The reference-shaped rows line up with the four playable character lanes. The EXP table is threshold-like, the growth-vars table is a seven-stat parameter row, and the initial-stats table carries startup experience, ten item slots, starting level, money, and a still-unresolved four-byte tail.

concepts.title: Level-Up Runtime
concepts.summary: `C1:D08B` is now the reusable `ComputeLevelUpStatGrowthDelta` helper. It is called seven times from `C1:D109`, once for each level-up stat lane, using the current base stat byte plus the per-character, per-stat growth-table byte. After each positive delta, `C1:D109` writes the stat increase back to the character record, calls the matching derived-stat refresh helper in bank C2, and optionally prints the corresponding level-up message.

concepts.title: Text And Selector Bridges
concepts.summary: The level-up narration path is strong because each stat-gain leaf dispatches a fixed EF message through the normal battle-text context machinery. Offense, defense, speed, guts, vitality, IQ, luck, max HP, and max PP all have distinct message anchors in the `EF:7A66..7B46` ladder. The statistic selector family at `C4:550F`, `C3:EE7A`, and `C1:9249` gives another bridge from character storage to text/display behavior. Selectors for level, current experience, HP/PP, and displayed stats now line up with concrete WRAM fields.

concepts.title: Open Edges
concepts.summary: The exact RNG/probability formula inside `C1:D08B` is still softer than the table role. The four unknown bytes at the end of each initial-stats row should remain literal until their startup consumer is followed. EXP threshold shape is strong, but the table should be presented as threshold data rather than as a complete level-up formula. Statistic-selector names are strongest for the late displayed-stat block; early fixed-width naming buffers still carry softer identities.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A growth editor should keep thresholds, growth variables, initial character state, derived-stat refresh, and level-up text together. Changing a growth byte is not just a data tweak; it affects the random delta helper, displayed derived stats, and visible narration. For now, expose the unresolved initial-stats tail and soft selector identities as preserved fields instead of inventing final names.

items.title: D5 Commerce And Shop Table Contracts
items.summary: How the D5 store inventory rows sit between item records, shop scripts, zero-terminated item slots, and unresolved shop-selector evidence.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Store Row Boundary
concepts.summary: `STORE_TABLE` is the first support table unlocked by the corrected item-table count. It starts immediately after the `254` item records at `D5:76B2`, has `66` rows, uses stride `0x07`, and ends at `D5:787F`. Each row is best treated as seven item-ID slots. Zero values act as empty slots in the reference-side inventory dump, while nonzero values point back into the corrected `ITEM_CONFIGURATION_TABLE` range. That makes a store row a compact list of sellable item IDs, not a standalone item definition.

concepts.title: Why The Item Boundary Matters
concepts.summary: The store table only becomes trustworthy after the item table boundary is corrected. If item rows were wrongly counted as `256`, the store table would be shifted and every shop inventory row would inherit a false address. That is why shop editing belongs near the item/equipment chapters. A shop row chooses item IDs; the item row supplies names, class bits, equipment slot behavior, battle item action fields, price-like fields, and menu behavior.

concepts.title: Selector Evidence Boundary
concepts.summary: The row range, row count, stride, and item-slot shape are strong from the D5 split and reference table shape. The consumer-side script selector is still thinner than the item and battle table families. The `ESHOP2` `0x19 0x20` note should not be overread as a broad shop-selector proof; it is a single mushroom-girl clinic helper that exposes a `$98A4` controller byte. Shop coverage becomes stronger when ordinary shop scripts are joined to concrete store row IDs and item-price/menu behavior.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A store row is seven item references plus the shop script or menu path that selects it. Item metadata stays in the item row, not duplicated inside the store row. Zero slots should be preserved as intentional empty inventory positions. Reordering item IDs is a shop inventory change; changing what an item does belongs to the item row contract.

items.title: D5 Condiment Table Contracts
items.summary: How food, condiment pairings, recovery amounts, effect classes, and the `APPLY_CONDIMENT` runtime path form a compact item-service contract.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Row Boundary
concepts.summary: `CONDIMENT_TABLE` is a compact D5 support table at `D5:EA77..D5:EBAA`. It has `44` rows, stride `0x07`, and sits after `STATS_GROWTH_VARS` and before the large map teleport destination table. The safest row model is a food item id, two compatible condiment item ids, an effect class byte, a good recovery amount, a bad recovery amount, and a runtime or timing byte. The reference-shaped rows label effect classes such as HP restore, PP restore, HP/PP restore, and random stat increase.

concepts.title: Runtime Path
concepts.summary: `APPLY_CONDIMENT` gives this table a stronger consumer story than many small support tables. The battle action argument supplies the food item id. The routine searches for a condiment in the current attacker's inventory, removes the matching condiment when found, and then walks the condiment rows until the food id matches. When the held condiment matches one of the row's two compatible condiment fields, the routine displays the successful seasoning text and returns a pointer into the row's effect/recovery fields. If the condiment is missing or mismatched, it displays the miss text and falls back to the ordinary item parameters for the food.

concepts.title: Contract Meaning
concepts.summary: Food and condiment item IDs are references into `ITEM_CONFIGURATION_TABLE`, not embedded item definitions. The two condiment fields are an either-or compatibility pair. The good and bad recovery bytes are behavior parameters selected by the condiment match outcome. The effect byte is stronger than a raw literal, but final user-facing names should stay tied to consumer behavior. The last byte is structurally part of the row; rows with nonzero values suggest timing/runtime policy and should remain cautiously labeled until followed locally.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A condiment editor should treat each row as a food-service rule: food item, compatible condiment options, effect class, good result, bad result, and preserved runtime byte. It should not edit food names, prices, inventory class bits, or battle item action words inside the condiment row. Because the runtime removes the matched condiment from the attacker before applying the row, the recovery behavior and inventory side effect belong together.

items.title: D5 Enemy Configuration Field Families
items.summary: How enemy configuration rows connect names, article flags, battle text pointers, music, final actions, rows, and battler initialization.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Row Identity
concepts.summary: `D5:9589` is the enemy configuration table. The row stride is `0x5E`, the table has `231` rows, local text extraction from `D5:9589 + 1 + n * 0x5E` yields enemy names, and local code indexes the family through a `#$005E` selector. The identity is now stronger than a reference-name match. Local battle setup maps enemy IDs through this table and initializes `0x4E`-byte battler rows at `9FAC + 0x4E * n`.

concepts.title: Battle Text Fields
concepts.summary: The two strongest pointer fields are `+0x2D` and `+0x31`. The current safest reads are encounter or battle-start text pointer for `+0x2D`, and KO or death text pointer for `+0x31`. Those names are reinforced by both local consumers and reference battle-flow order. The battle-start path prepares attacker-name context before displaying encounter text. The KO path displays death text before clearing enemy consciousness. That makes these fields part of the battle text pipeline, not generic script pointers.

concepts.title: Initializer Fields
concepts.summary: `C2:B6EB` is the local bridge from enemy ID to battler initialization. It builds `D5:9589 + enemy_id * 0x5E`, clears a `0x4E` battler struct, and copies enemy-data fields into battler fields such as sprite, article flag, row, HP, PP, and enemy ID copies. This upgrades the field names because they are consumed by live battler initialization, not just dumped from a reference struct. Enemy record fields now explain both storage and battle runtime state.

concepts.title: Strong Field Set
concepts.summary: `+0x00`: article or `the_flag` behavior, strengthened by name/article formatter paths. `+0x01..`: enemy name text field, locally extracted as readable enemy names. `+0x2D`: encounter or battle-start text pointer. `+0x31`: KO or death text pointer. `+0x37`: music or audio cue field. `+0x4E`: final action selector into the battle action descriptor family. `+0x54`: final action argument paired with the final action selector. `+0x5B`: row field used by row-aware battle text and battler initialization. `+0x5C`: max-called or call-for-help compatible limit. `+0x5D`: mirror-success threshold-like byte.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: Enemy rows should be edited as battle actors, not isolated stat blobs. A safe editor should show name/article fields, encounter/death text, battler initialization effects, battle action links, music, row placement, and any call/mirror behavior together. Fields without local consumers should remain positional or reference-assisted. The row identity is strong; that does not make every byte semantically final.

concepts.title: Main Result
concepts.summary: The D5 post-pad gameplay/table region `D5:5000..D5:FFFF` now reconciles exactly. The split report accounts for all `45056` bytes, with `21` split rows, a `62`-byte bounded unknown island at `D5:7A70`, and a `2287`-byte zero tail after the timed delivery table. That changes the editorial posture. D5 is no longer a broad blocked bank. It is a source-order table bank whose individual families can be promoted when their row shape, selector path, and runtime consumers are strong enough. That list is now broad enough to split the learning path. Battle and item rows have their own chapters; the smaller support families are promoted through shop, character-growth, and route/support chapters rather than remaining as a footnote in the split report.

concepts.title: Core Split Rows
concepts.summary: `ITEM_CONFIGURATION_TABLE`: `254` rows, stride `0x27`, span `D5:5000..D5:76B1`. `STORE_TABLE`: `66` rows, stride `0x7`, span `D5:76B2..D5:787F`. `PSI_TELEPORT_DEST_TABLE`: `16` rows, stride `0x1F`, span `D5:7880..D5:7A6F`. `BATTLE_ACTION_TABLE`: `318` rows, stride `0x0C`, span `D5:7B68..D5:8A4F`. `PSI_ABILITY_TABLE`: `54` rows, stride `0x0F`, span `D5:8A50..D5:8D79`. `ENEMY_CONFIGURATION_TABLE`: `231` rows, stride `0x5E`, span `D5:9589..D5:EA5A`. `TIMED_DELIVERY_TABLE`: `10` rows, stride `0x14`, span `D5:F649..D5:F710`.

concepts.title: Important Correction
concepts.summary: The item table has `254` rows, not `256`. At `0x27` bytes per row it ends at `D5:76B1`, and `STORE_TABLE` starts immediately at `D5:76B2`. This matters because every downstream item-field note should use the corrected table length and boundary. The split model also keeps `UNKNOWN_D57A70` as a bounded exact-boundary unknown instead of letting it pollute the surrounding teleport/contact/action families. Preserving small unknown islands is part of making the rest of the bank safer to teach.

concepts.title: Promotion Rule
concepts.summary: Use this chapter as the first stop for D5 field-family work. A family can be promoted when the split row gives exact range and stride, and another note proves who selects the row and what at least one field does. Do not promote all fields just because the row is reconciled. The split model proves storage. Consumer notes prove semantics.

items.title: D5 Item Action Field Families
items.summary: How item configuration fields drive broad classes, equipment slots, battle item actions, names, prompts, and targeting behavior.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Row Boundary
concepts.summary: `ITEM_CONFIGURATION_TABLE` starts at `D5:5000`, has `254` rows, and uses stride `0x27`. Item name display, inventory helpers, equipment helpers, text command checks, and battle item selection all depend on this boundary. The corrected row count matters because many item features are row-relative. A wrong end boundary would shift the store table and make every later D5 family harder to trust.

concepts.title: Packed Class Byte
concepts.summary: Byte `+0x19` is the strongest current item field. Bits `4..5` are broad item class, exposed through `C1:9EE6` as compact classes `1..4`. Bits `2..3` are the equipment slot subtype when the broad class indicates equippable gear. The unresolved parts are just as important: bits `0..1` and `6..7` should stay literal until caller-side evidence names them. The field is packed, but not every bit is known.

concepts.title: Battle Item Action Word
concepts.summary: The battle item resolver at `C1:CE85` indexes the item row, reads byte `+0x19`, and on the ordinary target-resolution path reads the item action word at `+0x1D`. That word is passed to the shared battle targeting resolver. This makes item action editing part of the same battle-facing model as PSI and action rows. An item row can choose inventory display behavior, equipment slot behavior, and battle targeting/action behavior through different fields.

concepts.title: Display Fields
concepts.summary: `C1:9216` prints item names from `ITEM_CONFIGURATION_TABLE`, using `0x19` bytes from the selected row. Nearby display helpers print PSI labels and wrap target prompts, which shows that item and PSI display share UI infrastructure even when their storage tables differ. For editor design, this is the bridge from storage to user-facing names. Name fields should be shown with their row provenance and text-display helper evidence, not as anonymous byte strings.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A safe item editor should show item name, packed class byte, equipment slot subtype, item action word, target resolver result, equipment compatibility, and relevant C3 inventory helper links together. Editing a battle item as if it were only an inventory name is too narrow. Keep unresolved class-byte bits as preserved bitfields. They are not junk; they are future field-family candidates.

items.summary: How PSI name rows, encoded C3 menu-entry rows, dynamic labels, and target prompt helpers connect PSI storage to visible battle/menu text.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: D5 Name Rows
concepts.summary: `PSI_NAME_TABLE` lives at `D5:8D7A..D5:8F22`, has `17` rows, and uses stride `0x19`. It is a fixed-width name table containing labels such as `PSI Fire`, `PSI Freeze`, `PSI Thunder`, `Lifeup`, `Healing`, `Shield`, `PSI Magnet`, and `Teleport`. These rows are display labels, not PSI ability definitions. The ability definition rows live separately at `D5:8A50`; the name rows become useful when C1 display helpers resolve a selector into a printable label.

concepts.title: Display Helper Split
concepts.summary: `C1:931B` is the general PSI or small dynamic label printer. Some selectors read fixed-width character-name buffers or the `$9819` dynamic buffer, while the ordinary PSI-label path uses the D5 PSI name table and fixed-length printing. `C1:CA06` is the cleaner PSI-id-plus-rank label builder. It reads `PSI_ID` and `PSI_LEVEL` from the `D5:8A50` ability row, maps the PSI id through the display path, and routes the rank through the adjacent C3 suffix-selection table.

concepts.title: Encoded Menu Entry Rows
concepts.summary: `C1:C8BC` builds the second-stage battle PSI menu entry row. It usually reads the associated `D5:7B68` battle action id from the ability row, uses the action row's first two selector bytes to compute a coarse offset into `C3:F124`, copies a 20-byte encoded row, appends the fixed `C3:F11C` tail, and then appends the PP cost. Thunder is the visible exception. When `PSI_ID == 4`, the routine bypasses the ordinary action-row-derived selector and indexes the encoded row table directly by the PSI-table row. The safest explanation is that the ordinary action-row selector is too coarse to uniquely choose Thunder's intended menu-entry row.

concepts.title: Prompt Boundary
concepts.summary: PSI display also touches targeting UI. `C1:93E7` opens and labels the temporary ally-target prompt before character selection, while `C1:9437` closes that prompt state afterward. These helpers are display scaffolding around targeting resolution, not PSI table storage. This is the recurring theme for PSI display: ability rows, name rows, encoded C3 rows, rank suffixes, PP-cost append behavior, and target prompt labels are connected evidence, but each piece has a different storage owner.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: Do not edit PSI name strings as if they alone define an ability. A PSI display edit should show the D5 ability row, D5 name row, C3 encoded menu-entry row, C3 suffix table, C1 display helper path, and any target prompt behavior that depends on the selected action. Keep the exact decode of C3 encoded row bytes visibly separate from the stronger facts: row width, copy length, selector path, Thunder bypass, and PP-cost append.

steps.title: Concepts To Track

concepts.title: Exact Support Spans
concepts.summary: `TELEPHONE_CONTACTS_TABLE`: `6` rows, stride `0x1F`, span `D5:7AAE..D5:7B67`. `TELEPORT_DESTINATION_TABLE`: `234` rows, stride `0x08`, span `D5:EBAB..D5:F2FA`. `MAP_HOTSPOTS`: `56` rows, stride `0x08`, span `D5:F2FB..D5:F4BA`. `TIMED_ITEM_TRANSFORMATION_TABLE`: `4` rows, stride `0x05`, span `D5:F4BB..D5:F4CE`. `DONT_CARE_NAMES`: `7` rows, stride `0x2A`, span `D5:F4CF..D5:F5F4`.

concepts.title: Route Versus Scene
concepts.summary: These tables are route/support data, not full map scenes. Teleport destination rows and hotspot rows need to be read beside the C0 teleport state machines, map-sector scene contracts, and script paths that select a destination. The storage spans are exact, but final field names should come from consumers. For example, a teleport row with eight bytes is not automatically a user-facing destination object until its selector path, coordinates, map-state changes, and arrival behavior are joined.

concepts.title: Name And Contact Data
concepts.summary: Telephone contacts and default names are text-adjacent support rows. Their row widths are reconciled, but their safest editor presentation should still preserve padding and fixed-width fields until the caller paths are fully joined to text rendering. The statistic-selector and naming-buffer notes are a useful caution here: fixed-width strings can be user-visible names, backing buffers, or dynamic text sources depending on the caller. The D5 support tables should keep storage width and display identity separate.

concepts.title: Timed Item Transformations
concepts.summary: The four-row timed item transformation table is structurally tiny but semantically important. It belongs near timed delivery and inventory work because its rows describe item-state changes over time rather than immediate item actions. Until a consumer note follows the transformation row fields end to end, the exact table span and likely inventory-service role are stronger than byte-by-byte field names.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: Route and support tables should be edited through the feature that selects them: teleport routing, phone menu/contact display, hotspot/map triggers, timed item changes, or naming defaults. Raw D5 rows are provenance, not the primary authoring interface. Route/support rows keep row IDs and fixed-width storage visible, while final field labels are reserved for values whose C0/C1/C3/C4 consumers have been followed.

steps.title: Start With The Narrative

items.title: D5 Service And Destination Field Families
items.summary: How landing destinations, timed delivery rows, row selectors, countdown/retry policy, success/failure pointers, and service latches fit together.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Landing Destinations
concepts.summary: `D5:7880` is best read as a fixed-stride landing-destination table. The stride is `0x1F`; the first `0x19` bytes are a padded destination name; words at `+0x1B` and `+0x1D` are destination-specific coarse coordinate words. Two local consumers prove the split. The text command path `0x1C 06 -> C1:46DE` prints the destination name. The landing-side consumer at `C0:DD79` reads the coordinate words, installs them into `$438A/$438C`, invalidates landing/profile caches, and drives world-side placement logic.

concepts.title: Timed Delivery Rows
concepts.summary: The timed delivery table is the D5 service row family at the end of the bank. It has `10` rows, stride `0x14`, and is now explained by a shared C3/EF controller rather than by table shape alone. The best current row sketch is: sprite or object descriptor, event-flag gate, retry threshold, retry wait in seconds, delivery countdown, immediate success pointer, deferred failure pointer, enter speed, and exit speed.

concepts.title: Row Selector Command
concepts.summary: Text command `[1F D3 xx]` is the script-side row selector for timed delivery. The byte `xx` behaves as a 1-based row number, so `[1F D3 01]` selects row `0`, `[1F D3 02]` selects row `1`, and so on through the ten known rows. The local handler now has a real path: the `0x1F D3` leaf returns callback low word `C1:7440`, and `C1:7440` forwards the selected row through `EF:0EAD`. That ties text-command selection to the EF delivery-row helper family.

concepts.title: Controller State
concepts.summary: The shared timed-delivery controller waits for the row-specific countdown, tests readiness through `EF:0F60`, retries using the row-specific threshold and wait policy, queues success pointer `1` on success, or queues failure pointer `2` after teardown. `EF:0FDB` begins success-side arrival state and sets both `$5D98` and `$5D9A`; `EF:0FF6` clears the transient arrival state and restores or resets the broader controller latch. `$5D98` is broader and more persistent, while `$5D9A` behaves more like an active-arrival or transient special-state flag.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: Landing destinations and timed-delivery rows should be edited as service records, not text-only labels. A destination row owns a printed name and world coordinates. A timed-delivery row owns policy, state, pointers, movement speeds, and text-command row selection. Row selector commands and D5 row fields belong together so a script's `[1F D3 xx]` command cannot drift away from the row it arms.

steps.title: Start With The Narrative
steps.summary: Read the chapter first so the evidence has context and confidence boundaries.

items.title: Item And Equipment Table Contracts
items.summary: How item records, packed class fields, battle item actions, equipment slots, menu helpers, and C3 inventory source units form an editing boundary.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Item Record Anchor
concepts.summary: The D5 split plan promotes the item table from a blocked bank region into a concrete table family. The key correction is that `ITEM_CONFIGURATION_TABLE` has `254` rows, not `256`; with `0x27` bytes per row it ends at `D5:76B1`, and the store table starts immediately at `D5:76B2`. That gives item work a stable row boundary. The next layer is field meaning, and the strongest current field is byte `+0x19`.

concepts.title: Packed Class Field
concepts.summary: Item byte `+0x19` is best read as a packed class-and-slot field. Bits `4..5` feed `C1:9EE6` as broad item classes, and bits `2..3` feed equipment-slot selection when the broad class says the item is equippable. The local behavior is strong: `C1:9EE6` masks `0x30` and converts the value into compact classes `1..4`, while `C1:9B79` requires class `2`, masks `0x0C`, and chooses one of four equipped-reference bytes in the selected character record. Bits `0..1` and `6..7` remain intentionally open.

concepts.title: Battle Item Boundary
concepts.summary: Battle item selection is the item-table counterpart to the PSI menu path. `C1:CFC6` opens the battle item-inventory selection loop, renders the acting character's inventory, stores the chosen slot, and calls `C1:CE85` to resolve the selected item. `C1:CE85` resolves the selected slot through C3 inventory helpers, indexes `ITEM_CONFIGURATION_TABLE` at `D5:5000`, reads byte `+0x19`, and then uses item action word `+0x1D` with the shared battle targeting resolver. This ties item records directly to battle action/target semantics rather than leaving them as inventory-only rows.

concepts.title: Equipment UI Boundary
concepts.summary: The item table does not stand alone. C1 equipment menu flows build comparison markers, render selected-character equipment lists, prepare equipment status displays, and run slot-selection loops. C2 and C4 helpers build preview rows and party equipment comparison visuals. C3 source units cover inventory, equipment, tracked items, and selector helpers. That means an equipment edit has a UI contract as well as a data contract. Changing class or slot fields can change whether a text command test succeeds, which equipped reference byte is read, which menu row appears, and which C3 helper path updates derived state.

concepts.title: Name And Prompt Display
concepts.summary: The C1 display helpers show why item, PSI, and targeting evidence belong near each other. `C1:9216` prints item names from `ITEM_CONFIGURATION_TABLE`. `C1:931B` prints PSI or small dynamic labels. `C1:93E7` and `C1:9437` open and close the target-selection prompt used by ally-targeting battle actions. For the encyclopedia, this means item table fields should link to display and target-prompt behavior when those paths are known. The row is storage; the display helper is evidence that a field is player-facing.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A safe item editor should treat item row, packed class bits, item action word, equipment slot subtype, text/menu command leaves, battle targeting resolver, equipment compatibility helpers, and derived preview state as one joined surface. The table row is the storage layer; the menu and C3 helper paths are the proof that a field is authoring-facing. Do not give unresolved bits a friendly name. Keep them visible as preserved fields until callers prove their meaning.
