concepts.title: Why This Page Exists
concepts.summary: Known limits are unresolved evidence boundaries. They mark where a generated page, table split, asset contract, or tool result is useful but not yet enough for a stronger claim. This page groups unresolved script semantics, fragile generated labels, incomplete data contracts, table fields that still need caller-side proof, and tooling results that should not be mistaken for ROM facts.

concepts.title: No Longer Limits
concepts.summary: Some items can now leave the broad unknown bucket. C3 event/actionscript parsing is closed at first-pass quality, several C3 value-family contracts are teachable, D5 post-pad table splitting is reconciled, the major D5 gameplay field families and smaller support-table families have first authored pages, condiment and PSI display rows have focused chapters, the map object bundle layer is usable, the map scene substrate has authored contract pages, the battle PSI ability table has a strong row model, and audio packs now have first stream and track snapshot contracts. Those are not finished editors. They are mature enough to be taught as contracts: the remaining work is field naming, value semantics, authoring UX, consumer-specific edge cases, and runtime proof where playback or rendering claims depend on hardware state.

concepts.title: Current Limit Categories
concepts.summary: Semantic names that are plausible but not proven. C3 callback arguments whose byte shape is known but whose helper-specific authoring meaning is still literal. C3 movement, direction, facing, and animation values that are family-local rather than global enums. Text/localization macros with strong structural lowering evidence but incomplete compiler-grade expansion rules. Runtime table fields with row-shape proof but only partial consumer-side names. Asset payloads with source ranges but no visual, structural, or runtime-selector fixture. ROM-backed enrichments that should remain optional local cache data. Generated pages that are useful references but not yet educational chapters. Map collision low bits `0x01/0x02`, DA palette metadata words, and text/common palette preview joining. Item byte `+0x19` low bits `0..1` and high bits `6..7`, plus battle/enemy table tail fields that still need caller-side proof. Audio pages that need a clear split between ROM facts, local ROM-derived outputs, and project playback/export tooling.

concepts.title: C3 Specific Limits
concepts.summary: Movement presets: pulse tasks and setup helpers are strong, while some `C0:A685` parameter pairs should remain literal until the underlying current-slot fields are named. Direction/facing: octant conversion and sprite-facing refresh behavior are proved, but player-visible labels for all `0..7` values and boundary-bias differences remain open. Animation templates: `V0` and `V4` roles are strong inside specific template families, but they should not be treated as universal variable names across all C3 scripts. Callback arguments: common schemas are now readable, but each friendly operand name still belongs to the target helper's evidence level. Source pilots: many source-form seams validate byte-for-byte, but some are intentionally not wired into the main C3 scaffold yet.

concepts.title: D5 Specific Limits
concepts.summary: D5 split model: row ranges and strides are reconciled, while `UNKNOWN_D57A70` remains a bounded exact-boundary unknown island. Battle action rows: early and many late families are teachable, but some tail rows and reference-assisted names still need caller-side proof before final symbolic promotion. Enemy rows: table identity, text pointers, row, final-action fields, and battler initialization links are strong, but not every `0x5E` byte has a local consumer name. Item rows: broad class bits, equipment slot subtype, name display, and battle action word are strong; unresolved packed bits should remain preserved literals. Service rows: landing destinations, timed delivery rows, shop inventory rows, character-growth rows, and route/support rows are now structured, but several fields still need deeper consumer-side proof before final naming.

concepts.title: Map Specific Limits
concepts.summary: Sector and scene rows are stable inventory roots, but ignored preview rendering still needs to be generated from local payloads. Ten sector-used tileset IDs have palette settings and scene use but no direct local `.fts` export. Palette descriptor slots `0..1` still belong to common/text palette space and need preview-tool joining. DA palette metadata words are structurally explained but not all runtime behavior is named. Collision low bits `0x01/0x02` are preserved surface modifier bits, not final gameplay labels. FTS animation/settings rows and EF/C0 tile-animation upload scripts are related but remain separate contract layers.

concepts.title: Audio Specific Limits
concepts.summary: Audio pack streams are now structurally parsed and validated, but internal sample, instrument, and sequence semantics remain a later layer. APU RAM seeds are diagnostic 64 KiB memory images, not complete `.spc` snapshots. Complete playback/export claims must identify the SPC700 CPU registers, DSP registers, timer/control state, APUIO mailbox state, driver-start timing, elapsed cycles, and capture source used by the renderer. Representative local playback/export now has validated SPC/WAV evidence, but that evidence is project tooling output, not checked-in ROM content. Generated `build/audio` outputs are ROM-derived local artifacts and stay ignored. The large `EE:9201..EE:FFFF` tail region remains an audio-bank boundary note rather than an explained authoring object.

concepts.title: Table Specific Limits
concepts.summary: Battle action table: early rows and several later C2 body families are strong, but some tail rows remain presentation-heavy or caller-thin. Enemy configuration table: row identity and several fields are strong, but not every `0x5E` field has local consumer names. PSI menu tables: D5 ability rows, PSI name rows, display helpers, and the main C1 helpers are strong, while `C3:F054..F0B0` and the exact decode of encoded C3 menu-entry rows remain softer internal splits. Item configuration table: row boundary, item name, broad class, equipment slot subtype, and battle item action word are strong; unresolved bitfields should remain literal. Map object tables: placement/object bundles are strong, but full event/actionscript semantics remain separate work.

concepts.title: Promotion Queue
concepts.summary: The strongest next promotions are narrow field-family chapters: NPC AI bytes, concrete shop selector paths, C3 encoded PSI menu row decoding, map preview/editor rules, audio runtime state capture, and eventually the sample/instrument/sequence split. Each promotion needs the same minimum shape: storage range, row or field width, direct consumers, reference-assisted names if used, remaining unknowns, and an editor-facing rule.

concepts.title: Source-Safe Boundary
concepts.summary: The recovered localization archive is local evidence, not checked-in content. The project can safely publish structural facts: file counts, hashes, labels, metadata fields, command inventories, cross-reference shapes, and semantic conclusions. It should not publish recovered message prose or copyrighted source text. Within that boundary, the archive is extremely useful. It supplies `57` `.MSG` files, `6049` labels including `3257` `MSG_*` labels, `202` unique authoring commands, and `45921` command occurrences. It also supplies `653` recovered metadata records that connect messages to object-like authoring context.

concepts.title: Record Shape
concepts.summary: The recurring record shape is the bridge from text to overworld behavior. Records include fields such as `;@Habitat`, `;@Person`, `;@Figure`, `;@AppearanceKey`, `;@ActionScript`, `;@GoodsMessage`, `;@CheckMessage`, and `;@Message`. Those fields can connect symbolic message labels to figures, appearance keys, object behavior, goods/check text, and action/event script selectors. That makes localization evidence relevant outside the text VM. It helps explain why an NPC is placed, what figure it uses, which message label it owns, and which action script or check/goods path belongs to the same authoring object.

concepts.title: Authoring Commands
concepts.summary: The authoring command frontier classifies all known `.MSG` commands. Some lower directly to runtime VM commands. Some are source formatting conveniences. Others are display, movement, inventory, query, status, battle, or control macros that need expansion evidence before they become editor-facing controls. The current frontier records no still-unclassified commands. That does not mean all commands are fully lowered. It means each command has a responsible bucket, which is the necessary first step for safer authoring tools.

items.title: Localization Control Macro Lowering
items.summary: How recovered `.MSG` control macros likely lower into existing text VM control, memory, register, menu, and branch commands.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Model
concepts.summary: Recovered control macros are source-level conveniences over the existing bank-01 text VM. They are not evidence for a separate runtime VM. Direct controls such as `@GOSUB`, `@GOTO`, `@TRUE_GOTO`, `@FALSE_GOTO`, and `@CHKFGOTO` map naturally to runtime control behavior. Register, comparison, loop, and multi-way branch helpers require lowering hypotheses. This model keeps the authoring language useful without inventing runtime machinery. The source macro is what a local author wrote; the lowered command sequence is what the game executes.

concepts.title: Strong Motifs
concepts.summary: The strongest evidence comes from repeated adjacent motifs. `@CMP > @ONGOSUB` appears `254` times and has the inverse pairing count recorded in the same debug corpus. `@SET_LOOPREG > @GOSUB` appears `191` times across `31` files. `@DSP_ITEM > @SELGOTO` appears `188` times across `35` files. These motifs are stronger than one-off command guesses because they show how source commands are composed. They should be taught as lowering patterns with confidence notes, not as isolated aliases.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: Text editing preserves the difference between direct runtime commands and recovered authoring macros. If a command has a direct runtime equivalent, it can be shown as a command. If it expands through register setup, comparison, menu display, or branch table selection, it remains a macro with a visible lowering profile. Where a lowering hypothesis is plausible but not final, keep the source macro name, runtime bytes, motif evidence, and uncertainty together. That gives users a useful editing model without silently baking in a guess.

steps.summary: Read the chapter first so the evidence has context and confidence boundaries.

items.title: Map Collision Runtime Contracts
items.summary: How FTS collision bytes, D8 collision pointer records, C0 runtime masks, terrain compatibility bits, and unresolved low bits should be read.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Storage Model
concepts.summary: The third byte of each `.fts` arrangement cell is storage-verified as the tile collision or behavior byte. D8 collision pointer entries match `.fts` collision records exactly, so the storage side is high confidence. The meaningful uncertainty is no longer where collision bytes live. It is which gameplay names should be assigned to each bit after following runtime masks and callers.

concepts.title: Runtime Masks
concepts.summary: `0x00C0`: high collision/block mask used by player, bicycle, pathfinding, teleport, and movement-script probes. `0x00D0`: movement cache stop mask, combining high collision with the `0x10` special-surface latch bit. `0x0010`: special surface coordinate latch; C0 stores probed coordinates for later movement handling. `0x000C`: entity terrain compatibility class bits consumed through entity metadata compatibility checks. `0x003F`: returned surface modifier mask, preserving low six bits after stripping high collision bits.

concepts.title: Known And Open Bits
concepts.summary: `0x80` is the observed solid/high-collision bit in verified D8 and `.fts` data. `0x40` is runtime-supported by the high-collision mask but not observed in verified map collision data. `0x10` participates in special-surface coordinate latching. `0x04` and `0x08` feed entity terrain compatibility. Low bits `0x01` and `0x02` remain preserved surface modifier bits. They are counted, returned, and runtime-visible, but they should not receive strong human gameplay labels until caller-side evidence proves them.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A collision editor should expose proved masks as behavior groups while preserving the raw byte. Users need to see both the practical labels and the bit-level storage because some bits participate in multiple masks. Do not collapse collision into a single solid/not-solid checkbox. The runtime distinguishes high blocking, movement cache stops, special-surface latches, terrain compatibility, and returned surface modifiers.

items.title: Map Object Table Contracts
items.summary: How map placements, NPC config rows, sprite contracts, movement IDs, event pointers, text fields, doors, and palette tables become world-editing data.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Object Bundle Row
concepts.summary: The practical world-editing unit is now the map object bundle row. It joins placed-object identity, NPC config, sector and world-pixel position, NPC type, visibility rule, initial direction, sprite ID, palette, runtime slot count, movement ID, C4 pointer target, event flag, and text fields. Current coverage is strong: `1584` NPC config rows are joined to visual metadata, `1582` placements are exposed as stable `map_object.NNNN` rows, `627` of `1280` sectors contain placed objects, and all `895` C4 event pointer-table targets are decoded to concrete addresses.

concepts.title: Behavior Boundary
concepts.summary: The object layer is intentionally a table contract, not a full event VM decompilation. It proves behavior entrypoints, macro profiles, source-file coverage, pointer targets, and object usage. Full event/actionscript semantics live in the C3 chapters. The remaining `21` placed objects without present reference script files are no longer address-unknown. They are compact late movement IDs with C3 targets from `C3:9623` through `C3:9A28`, and sampled scripts follow a repeated template.

concepts.title: Scene Substrate
concepts.summary: Objects need a surface. The next layer joins sectors, doors, rope/ladder/stair/escalator/switch/person/object triggers, enemy-map groups, music options, hotspots, map-change counts, tileset IDs, palette settings, and sector hashes. The map palette pointer contract is a good example of a table promoted all the way to a contract: `32` long-pointer entries, `96` table bytes, exact pointer-to-palette asset matches, no palette-setting mismatch, and `28` palette assets used by sectors.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A map object editor should never ask users to edit a placement row in isolation. The safe authoring object is the joined bundle: placement, NPC config, sprite, palette, movement, script target, visibility flag, interaction text, and scene substrate. When localization metadata supplies `;@Figure`, `;@AppearanceKey`, `;@ActionScript`, goods/check/message pointers, or symbolic `MSG_*` labels, treat that as crosswalk evidence. It can strengthen the object contract, but ROM-backed placement and pointer evidence remain the storage authority.

steps.title: Start With The Narrative
steps.summary: Read the chapter first so the evidence has context and confidence boundaries.

items.title: Map Palette Contracts
items.summary: How DA palette assets, `.fts` palette variant rows, palette pointer tables, descriptor palette fields, and script palette commands connect.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Palette Variant Rows
concepts.summary: The `.fts` `290`-character rows are now resolved as map palette variant rows. Each row has a two-character ID and a `288`-character payload that decodes to `96` SNES BGR555 words, or `192` bytes, arranged as six subpalettes of sixteen colors. All `168` `.fts` palette rows match palette-setting keys. `129` match raw ROM palette variants exactly, and `39` match after reserved metadata zeroing. There are no unexplained mismatches.

concepts.title: DA Pointer Table
concepts.summary: The DA map palette pointer table at `DA:FAA7..DA:FB07` is a `32`-entry long-pointer table. Each entry points exactly at the corresponding `MAP_DATA_PALETTE_N` asset, with `96` table bytes and `32` exact pointer/asset matches. This closes the storage identity. It does not by itself name every metadata word or explain every palette command effect, which is why the descriptor and command notes remain separate evidence layers.

concepts.title: Descriptor Boundary
concepts.summary: Descriptor palettes `2..7` map to the six DA map-palette subpalettes. Descriptor palettes `0..1` belong to text/common palette space and still need the common/text palette source joined into preview tooling. Reserved palette words in raw DA variants carry metadata-like settings: event flag, event palette selector, sprite palette, and flash effect slots. The `.fts` visual rows zero those slots, which explains the exact mismatch class without turning the metadata words into fully named runtime behavior.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A map palette editor should separate visual color rows from reserved metadata words and script-side palette command behavior. A preview can use the zeroed `.fts` visual row, but a ROM patcher must preserve or intentionally edit the DA metadata slots. Do not treat descriptor palettes `0..1` as missing map colors. They are a known boundary with the common/text palette layer.

items.summary: How sectors, tilesets, .fts exports, palette variants, tile animations, collision records, placed objects, and palette commands form the map asset layer.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Why Map Assets Are Different
concepts.summary: The map layer is not a pile of independent graphics. A scene needs sector identity, placed objects, triggers, doors, hotspots, enemy groups, music, map-change counts, tileset dependencies, palette variants, arrangement cells, collision records, tile animation records, and runtime palette command behavior. The current milestone turns those scattered facts into a reproducible set of checked-in contracts. The contracts are payload-free but detailed enough to define scene bundles.

concepts.title: Closed Contract Stack
concepts.summary: All `1280` world sectors have stable sector inventory rows. Placed objects are joined from object bundles into the sector layer. The full `0..31` tileset ID domain is mapped, with `28` IDs used by sectors and `20` direct `.fts` exports present. Direct `.fts` exports share a stable `64/290/96` section shape. Arrangement records decode as 2-byte SNES BG tilemap descriptor words plus a 1-byte collision attribute. All `168` variable 290-character rows are verified as DA palette variants with no unexplained mismatches. EF tile-animation graphics/script pointer tables and C0 `$43DC` upload records are joined for `20` animation IDs. D8 collision pointer entries match `.fts` collision records exactly, and C0 runtime masks ground the major collision bit roles.

concepts.title: Scene Bundle Shape
concepts.summary: `map_scene.NNNN` is the scene-bundle root. Under it sit sector metadata, map object IDs, trigger/door/hotspot context, enemy/music context, `map_tileset.NN`, palette variant rows, tile animation records, arrangement/collision records, and preview hashes. This is already enough to begin designing a native loader boundary. It is not yet a claim that every visual pixel or collision low bit is semantically named.

concepts.title: Palette And Collision Boundaries
concepts.summary: The palette contracts prove that descriptor palettes `2..7` map to the six DA map-palette subpalettes and that descriptor palettes `0..1` belong to text/common palette space. The palette command contract verifies all parsed `CHANGE_MAP_PALETTE` hits against resolved palette variants. The collision contracts prove the storage side and the major runtime masks. Observed solid/high collision is `0x80`; `0x10` latches special-surface coordinates; `0x04/0x08` feed entity terrain compatibility; low bits `0x01/0x02` remain intentionally unnamed until caller-side gameplay labels are proven.

concepts.title: Known Limits
concepts.summary: Ten sector-used tileset IDs currently have palette settings without direct local `.fts` exports. Descriptor palettes `0..1` still need the common/text palette source joined into preview tooling. DA palette metadata words have structural names but need runtime behavior follow-up. Collision low bits `0x01/0x02` are preserved and counted but should not receive strong names yet. Scene previews are ignored local outputs; the checked-in contract is the source-safe layer.

concepts.title: Sector Root

concepts.title: Scene Composition
concepts.summary: `map_scene.NNNN` rows join the sector inventory to tileset and palette status. The current scene composition contract covers all `1280` scenes, `28` used tilesets, `950` direct-FTS scenes, and `330` palette-settings-only scenes. The scene contract deliberately stores hashes, counts, dependency status, and feature counts instead of raw tile grids. Preview/build tools can regenerate scene payloads locally while the encyclopedia stays source-safe.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A map scene editor should use the scene row as the root. Editing an object, door, palette, tile animation, collision cell, music override, or enemy group should keep the sector row visible so the user understands the full scene context. The current contract is an inventory and dependency layer, not a finished renderer. The next renderer can attach ignored preview outputs to these scene IDs without changing the source-safe schema.

concepts.title: Runtime Model
concepts.summary: The map tile-animation runtime is now a ROM-verified contract. Selector `$4372` chooses entries from EF graphics and upload-script pointer tables. Graphics decompress into `7E:C000`, upload scripts expand into `$43DC` runtime records, and C0 drives VRAM transfer through the documented upload path. The active runtime pair covers `20` animation IDs, with `20` graphics pointer/asset matches, `24` upload-script records, `12` nonempty scripts, and `8` empty placeholder scripts.

concepts.title: Upload Records
concepts.summary: Each 8-byte upload-script record expands to a 16-byte runtime record. The fields are frame count limit, reload delay, transfer size, source base offset, VRAM destination, live countdown, live frame counter, and live source offset. All scripts fit the `$43DC` runtime capacity, all scripts end at the next pointer, and the script data ends at the sprite grouping table start. That makes the active EF/C0 runtime table pair closed at the structural level.

concepts.title: FTS Boundary
concepts.summary: The `.fts` animation/settings rows are related but not identical to the C0 runtime upload scripts. Their row counts do not equal the decoded upload-script record counts, so they should remain a separate export-layer contract. The runtime upload records that drive VRAM transfer and the `.fts` settings rows in the exported tileset package are related but separate evidence layers.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: Tile-animation editing must keep graphics asset, upload script, scene dependency, and VRAM destination together. Editing only the decompressed graphics can desynchronize the runtime script that copies it. Placeholder-empty entries are meaningful too. The contract records tiny placeholder payload IDs and empty scripts so tools can distinguish intentionally inactive animation IDs from missing data.

items.summary: How tileset IDs, direct `.fts` exports, palette-settings-only rows, tile pixels, arrangement/collision records, and animation/settings rows fit together.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Tileset Domain
concepts.summary: The map tileset domain is `0..31`. `28` IDs are used by sectors, `20` direct `.fts` exports are present in the local refs, and `18` used IDs have direct exports. Ten used IDs currently have palette settings and sector use but no direct local `.fts` export. The contract records that gap directly. It does not invent a mapping for palette-settings-only IDs, which is exactly the right source-safe behavior.

concepts.title: FTS Shape
concepts.summary: All present `.fts` exports share a stable `64/290/96` section shape. The `64`-character rows are high-confidence 8x8 indexed tile pixel rows. The variable `290`-character rows are palette or animation/settings-shaped rows. The `96`-character rows decode as arrangement/collision records. The format audit covers `20` direct exports, all matching the current shape, with `1024` tile-pixel rows and `1024` arrangement/collision rows per export.

concepts.title: Arrangement Cells
concepts.summary: The `96`-character section decodes as `1024` records per tileset, each record holding `16` three-byte cells in a `4x4` grid. The first two bytes in each cell behave as a little-endian SNES BG tilemap descriptor word. The third byte is the collision or behavior attribute byte. Across `20` tilesets the arrangement contract represents `20480` records and `327680` cells. Descriptor words yield tile index, palette, priority, horizontal flip, and vertical flip fields in the standard SNES tilemap shape.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: A tileset editor should treat FTS tile pixels, arrangement/collision cells, palette variants, and animation/settings rows as related but separate layers. The `96`-row section is not just art; it owns collision attributes too. For palette-settings-only tileset IDs, show the dependency gap honestly. A scene can be known and palette-backed without having a direct local `.fts` export yet.

items.summary: How D1-D5 sprite payloads become object-facing contracts through sprite groups, runtime slots, animation roles, map placements, movement IDs, and behavior targets.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Mental Model
concepts.summary: D1-D5 contain overworld sprite graphics payloads, but the game does not place raw graphics payloads on the map. It places objects. The object-facing contract joins a visual identity, runtime frame slots, animation-role names, map placement, movement/script behavior, event flags, and text pointers. That is the important promotion: sprite payloads become useful to tools only after the project can answer what object uses them, where it appears, which runtime slot model selects its frames, and which behavior entrypoint controls it.

concepts.title: Join Layers
concepts.summary: Sprite group contracts map ebsrc `SPRITE_GROUP_*` labels onto D1-D5 payload assets and EBDecomp metadata. Frame contracts resolve EF `spritepointerarray` runtime slots to concrete D1-D5 payload assets and low-bit renderer effects. Animation role contracts promote slot order into direction, phase, descriptor-pass, and palette roles. Map sprite usage joins NPC config rows and map placements to sprite metadata and direct EF runtime slot records. Map movement usage joins NPC movement IDs to C4 pointer-table targets and C3 event/actionscript refs. Map object bundles combine those layers into stable `map_object.NNNN` rows.

concepts.title: Current Closure
concepts.summary: The object layer is closed enough for editor and port work. The local notes report `1582` placed object rows, `1584` NPC config rows joined to visual metadata, `627` populated sectors, `297` unique NPC sprite IDs, and `136` used movement IDs. Only sprite `0`, `OVERWORLD_SPRITE::NONE`, remains metadata-only. The remaining late movement scripts are not address-unknown: `21` placed objects point at known C3 target addresses whose expected ref script files are absent. That should be treated as a compact script-emission frontier, not a failure of the object asset model.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: For an object editor, the primary row should be the placed object bundle, not the raw sprite payload. A user wants to know what is placed here, what it looks like, what behavior entrypoint it uses, and what interaction fields are attached. The D1-D5 graphics are one dependency under that row. For an art tool, the primary row can be the sprite group or animation-role contract, but it still needs to preserve runtime slot order, pointer-bit descriptor-pass behavior, and palette role metadata so edited art remains compatible with the renderer.

concepts.title: Known Limits
concepts.summary: Object contracts identify behavior entrypoints, but they do not fully decompile every event/actionscript payload. Some late movement IDs need generated script assets or reconstructed source files. Sprite animation roles are stable tool-facing labels derived from slot position; group-specific animation semantics still need care. Composed overworld previews are prototype outputs under ignored build folders, not committed canonical assets.

items.title: Overworld Walking Stutter Truth State
items.summary: Current reconciled model for the overworld walking microstutter: camera and scroll publication are mostly cleared, strip dedupe helped but was incomplete, and the companion visual `A750 -> A794` watcher rerun seam is the leading patch target.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Current Model
concepts.summary: The current stutter model has shifted away from stale camera state or stale scroll publication. The live camera step path, runtime scroll shadow writes, alternating NMI shadow publication, and NMI PPU scroll commit path now look healthy in the tested walking cases. The visible hitch is better explained as aggregate presentation workload. The strip-upload family is real and still contributes, but the strongest remaining patchable sub-family is the companion visual lane around `C0:A794`, especially the broader watcher-side rerun site at `C0:A750`.

concepts.title: Producer Split
concepts.summary: The walking refresh umbrella around `C0:1558` has two useful visual producer families. The known strip lane reaches `C0:0E16`, `C0:0FCB`, and `C0:1181`, producing map or strip uploads in bands such as `58xx` and `5Cxx`. A separate companion/entity visual lane flows through `C0:2A50 -> C0:2957 -> C0:1E49`, seeds tile-base fields such as `$298E`, and later reaches `C0:1CA8` plus `C0:A4C4/A794`. That split explains why strip dedupe could help without solving the hitch. Diagonal walking can activate both axis lanes and both visual families in the same frame, so the remaining problem is not necessarily a single bad upload. It may be too much legitimate per-frame presentation work.

concepts.title: Cleared Or Downgraded
concepts.summary: `C0:8012` is startup-only, not a frame pacing seam. `C0:834E` is NMI bookkeeping, not a main-loop wait seam. `C0:17EA..18F2`, `C0:1558`, `C0:8B20..8B8D`, and `C0:8284..82CA` now form a healthier camera-to-scroll-publication chain than the older stale-scroll theory allowed. The queue-overflow spin loop at `C0:8671..8673` is downgraded because it did not trigger during visible stutter in the safe-v2 test. The timer-only `A6E3` gate was safe but too narrow to visibly matter.

concepts.title: Leading Patch Seam
concepts.summary: The best current patch seam is the common watcher-side rerun at `C0:A750`, above `A794` but below the broad companion watcher family. It is broader than the failed timer-only experiment and safer than hooking shared queue helpers such as `A56E`, `8643`, `8616`, or `865F`. The compare tuple should not be only `$341A + $10F2`. The current notes call for a fuller derived descriptor signature: raw descriptor header, VRAM base `$298E`, transfer size `$2A7E`, transfer count `$2ABA`, source bank or auxiliary-prepass state from `$2A42/$2BAA`, and the effective selector pointer from `$29CA + 4*DATA_C0A623[$2AF6] + $10F2`.

concepts.title: Best Decomp Follow-Up
concepts.summary: The best render-side decomp seam is now downstream of smooth camera motion: `C0:7B52..7C5A -> C0:A780 -> C0:A794`. The visible-entry refresh computes screen-space coordinates from the smooth camera shadows and then enters the same companion descriptor family. If patching pauses and decomp resumes first, the next sampling pass should separate `C0:8677` traffic by upstream family: direct `1CA8/1D15`, `A56E -> 8643` split by `A4C4` versus `A794`, and the strip family `0E16/0FCB/1181`.

concepts.title: Working Rule
concepts.summary: Do not return to timer-only gating as the main experiment. Do not jump into `A56E`, `8643`, `8616`, or `865F` as a first patch target. Prefer the broader `A750` watcher-side gate with the fuller derived descriptor tuple. Treat camera and scroll publish as mostly cleared until new traces contradict that. Keep strip-family refinements as a later target after the companion-side rerun seam is tested.

concepts.title: Backend Policy
concepts.summary: The backend adapter is project infrastructure, not a ROM-content contract. It consumes payload-free job descriptions and local ROM-derived artifacts, then records whether a renderer produced valid state captures, SPC snapshots, WAV/PCM, metrics, or comparison data. `ares` is the accuracy-first emulator lane. `snes_spc`/libgme is the lightweight render lane for suitable SPC snapshots. External reference captures from bsnes/higan, Mesen2, or Mednafen remain optional comparison tools.

concepts.title: Artifact Boundaries
concepts.summary: `renderer_fixture` describes the job and points to ignored APU RAM seeds and pack transcripts; it must not embed ROM-derived bytes. `apu_ram_seed` is a raw 65536-byte local diagnostic image and remains ignored. `backend_job` indexes backend, track, fixture, output paths, and expected modes without carrying ROM payloads. `backend_result` records status, hashes, diagnostics, and paths to outputs such as state captures, complete SPC snapshots, WAV/PCM, and reference comparisons. `playback_export_manifest` collects validated local WAV/SPC outputs into an app-facing handoff object without making those outputs distributable. Validation checks schema, output existence, byte counts, SHA-1 hashes, headers, render metrics, and quality gates. Accuracy claims still depend on the stated runtime-state source and comparison scope.

concepts.title: Result Status
concepts.summary: The result schema supports `ok`, `failed`, `unsupported`, and `mismatch`. Those labels are scoped to the job's declared mode: a protocol dry run can be `ok` for shape, while a playback/export job is `ok` only when it writes validated audio/state outputs. The useful diagnostics are execution mode, handshake policy, timing basis, output hashes, backend version, source-state label, and reference capture identity. They make local experiments reproducible without turning backend implementation details into ROM facts.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: Editor-facing audio contracts stay centered on ROM pack and track semantics. Backend adapters are replaceable local playback/export lanes that consume those contracts and report their own evidence.

items.title: PSI Menu And Ability Table Contracts
items.summary: How D5 PSI ability rows, C1 menu helpers, C3 PSI menu data tables, and battle action rows form a joined PSI editing model.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Ability Row
concepts.summary: `D5:8A50` is best read as the battle PSI ability table with 15-byte rows. Row `0` is a zeroed dummy and rows `1..52` behave as live PSI abilities. The strongest fields are PSI ID, PSI level, category, target, associated battle action ID, Ness/Paula/Poo learn levels, menu X/Y placement, and description pointer. The row is both menu metadata and battle behavior glue. It names and places a PSI ability in menus, but it also points to a `D5:7B68` battle action row that supplies action metadata such as targeting behavior, PP/cost, message pointer, and handler pointer.

concepts.title: Menu Data Corridor
concepts.summary: The C3 corridor `C3:EF26..F1EC` is now table-shaped rather than raw decorative data. It contains selector group tables, group slice counts, a softer render-metadata-and-label block, a seven-by-seven known-state gate table, rank suffix data, a fixed menu-entry tail, and the PSI menu-entry row table. The strongest C3 tables are directly indexed by C1 helpers: `C1:C046` reads the selector group table, `C1:C0B6` reads group slice counts, and `C1:C165` scans known PSI state through the gate table. `C3:F054..F0B0` remains a block contract because its exact field split is still softer than the byte and word tables around it.

concepts.title: C1 Helper Path
concepts.summary: The C1 menu path is now source-backed enough to teach. `C1:C8BC` formats PSI menu entry rows over `D5:8A50`, usually deriving display shape through the associated `D5:7B68` action row. `C1:C853` resolves deeper PSI targeting metadata and may also hand off into ordinary action-row behavior. The Thunder special case is an important example of why this is a contract rather than a simple table dump. The ordinary action-row-derived selector appears too coarse for Thunder's intended menu-entry row, so the formatter bypasses by PSI ID in that case.

concepts.title: Display And Prompt Boundary
concepts.summary: PSI names, small dynamic labels, and target prompts share display helpers with item and battle targeting paths. `C1:931B` prints PSI or small dynamic labels, while `C1:93E7` and `C1:9437` wrap the ally-target prompt setup and cleanup used by targeting resolution. This makes PSI editing a UI/data/runtime problem at the same time. The useful view connects ability rows, action rows, C3 menu-row data, C1 display helpers, and targeting prompt behavior.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: Do not edit PSI menu text, learn levels, target class, PP behavior, and action handler as separate isolated things. The safe PSI editing unit is the joined row: D5 ability metadata, associated D5 action row, C3 menu display data, C1 menu helper behavior, and EF/E0 text payload references. The remaining soft edge is mostly the C3 render-metadata-and-label block and any places where action-row-derived display behavior is coarser than the PSI family name a user expects.

items.title: Table Contract Model
items.summary: How runtime tables become source-safe, editor-facing contracts: row shape, selectors, consumers, provenance, and edit boundaries.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Contract Shape
concepts.summary: A table contract is the durable explanation for a repeated data family. It records where the table lives, how wide each row is, how many rows are live, which code selects a row, what each proven field means, and what can be safely changed without breaking adjacent data. This is different from naming a blob. A blob can be source-safe and still be semantically thin. A contract needs row shape, selector evidence, runtime consumers, pointer ownership, validation status, and an explicit uncertainty boundary.

concepts.title: Evidence Ladder
concepts.summary: Byte budget: the table range reconciles with bank padding, neighbors, and source-order splits. Row shape: stride, live row count, and tail bytes are stable. Selector path: callers index the table through a known ID, pointer, row number, or runtime slot. Consumer path: fields are read by named code paths, not just guessed from repeated values. Crosswalk: reference-source or local extraction evidence can strengthen names, but should be labeled as such. Editor boundary: the contract says which fields are safe, which are literal, and which remain reserved or unresolved.

concepts.title: Current Strong Families
concepts.summary: The strongest current table families are clustered around D5 gameplay data, map object bundles, map palette pointers, C3 late interaction tables, battle action and PSI ability records, enemy configuration records, item/equipment classification fields, shop inventories, character growth/start state, route/support tables, condiment rows, and PSI name/display rows. D5 is especially important because its `D5:5000..D5:FFFF` post-pad region is now fully reconciled: `45056` bytes accounted, `20` table or tail rows in the split report, a named zero island, and a zero tail. That turns the bank from a broad unresolved region into a set of table families that can be promoted one by one.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: The safe edit unit for a table is usually a row plus its selector and consumer context. Changing an enemy field is not just changing a byte in D5; it can affect name formatting, battle text pointers, music, actions, row placement, and mirror or call-for-help behavior. Changing an item field can affect text VM checks, equipment slot selection, menu display, and C3 inventory helpers. Promote table fields conservatively. A field with one local consumer can receive a local behavior name. A field with local consumers plus a clean reference crosswalk can receive a stronger authoring name. Fields that are only positionally plausible should stay literal until the next consumer is proven.

items.title: Text Command Family Model
items.summary: How top-level text commands, structured subcommand families, and parser-only pseudo-opcodes should be read.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: Top Level
concepts.summary: The text VM manifest tracks `32` top-level command IDs. Most are runtime commands with direct parser behavior. Three `0x15..0x17` entries are parser-only pseudo-opcodes for compressed-bank handling and should not be taught as ordinary text authoring commands. This is the first sorting rule for a reader: a command entry can be a runtime operation, a gateway into a subcommand family, or a parser artifact. The same numeric style does not guarantee the same kind of edit.

concepts.title: Structured Families
concepts.summary: The dense part of the system lives under `0x18..0x1F`. The current family model tracks window management, data and substitution, menu and selection, memory context, print/display, inventory and money checks, stat recovery, and deferred callbacks/events. Across those families the manifest tracks `203` subcommands. Coverage varies by family. Some leaves are fully explained, some are runtime-only, and a few are artifact candidates where the parser evidence exists but the authoring story is not stable. That variation should stay visible in the generated entry rather than being flattened into a single confidence value.

concepts.title: Editing Rule
concepts.summary: When a text command starts a family, edit the family leaf, not just the parent opcode. The parent tells the parser where to dispatch. The leaf often decides the actual behavior: window state, actor display, inventory check, status recovery, event callback, branch, substitution, or menu handling. A safe command-family entry names the parent, leaf ID, argument shape, runtime behavior, authoring aliases if known, coverage status, and any macro-lowering relationship. Unknown fields stay directly labeled as unknown.

steps.title: Concepts To Track
steps.summary: Keep these ideas in mind while reading notes and generated references.

concepts.title: System Shape
concepts.summary: The text system has two overlapping layers: the runtime command VM that the game executes, and the recovered localization authoring language that lowered source-like `.MSG` records into that runtime format. Treating them as one thing hides important safety rules. Treating them as unrelated misses the best evidence bridge in the project. The current manifest decodes `61` text segments and tracks `32` top-level runtime commands. `29` top-level commands are covered by semantic notes, while `3` entries are parser-only compressed-bank pseudo-opcodes. The structured family layer covers `8` command families and `203` tracked subcommands.

concepts.title: Evidence Layers
concepts.summary: Runtime opcode layer: command IDs such as `0x18` through `0x1F`, their argument shapes, and their parser behavior. Family leaf layer: subcommands under structured families such as window management, data substitution, menu selection, inventory checks, recovery, and deferred callbacks. Authoring syntax layer: recovered `.MSG` commands, metadata records, labels, and comments from the localization source archive. Macro lowering layer: hypotheses that connect source-level control, register, menu, and branch macros to runtime VM bytes. Artifact boundary layer: parser-only pseudo-opcodes, source formatting commands, and locally ignored recovered material that should not be treated as runtime semantics.

concepts.title: Editing Rules
concepts.summary: Do not assume every `0xNN xx` spread is a command family; top-level opcodes, family subcommands, parser artifacts, and authoring macros have different meanings. Use runtime command entries for exact byte lookup, this chapter for the system model, and localization chapters for source-authoring syntax. Use macro lowering notes when recovered authoring commands and runtime bytes disagree, especially for branches, loops, registers, inventory display, and menu selection. Keep `.MSG` source metadata public-safe: structural counts, labels, command inventories, and semantic summaries are useful; recovered copyrighted source text stays local and ignored. Promote a text edit only when the affected runtime command, family leaf, macro lowering profile, and bank-local payload ownership are all clear.

concepts.title: Where The Evidence Lives
concepts.summary: The evidence is spread across top-level command manifests, localization authoring frontiers, macro lowering profiles, and individual command notes. This chapter is the stable reading path through those pieces, while the related chapters split out the command-family model, recovered authoring format, and control-macro lowering story.

entries.title: Local Workspace
entries.summary: Select and verify a user-provided ROM, create a local app-data workspace, and generate ROM-derived artifacts outside the shipped app.
entries.body:
The local workspace is the app boundary between source-safe knowledge and ROM-derived generated artifacts.

## First Run
- Open the encyclopedia without a ROM to read project-authored notes and contracts.
- Select an EarthBound ROM to verify size, header status, and SHA-1.
- A verified ROM creates a hash-keyed app-data workspace for generated source, assets, audio, previews, manifests, cache files, and export bundles.

## Verification Contract
- Expected headerless size: `3145728` bytes.
- Expected headered size: `3146240` bytes; the first 512 bytes are ignored for identity checks.
- Expected headerless SHA-1: `d67a8ef36ef616bc39306aa1b486e1bd3047815a`.

## Policy
- Checked in: App shell, curated docs, payload-free contracts, generators, validators, and public manifests.
- Generated locally: ROM-derived source, assets, audio, previews, cache files, and export bundles live in the user's local workspace.
- Never distributed: ROM bytes, raw extracted copyrighted assets, generated SPC/WAV/PNG payloads, and generated byte-equivalent source.

Use the live controls on this page in the Electron app to add or replace a ROM. The static browser build can still be used in notes-only mode.

entries.title: Release Artifact Policy
entries.summary: What belongs in the shipped encyclopedia app, what is generated locally, and what must never be distributed.
entries.body:
The release boundary is intentionally conservative. The app should publish knowledge, contracts, generators, and validators; the user's ROM should produce protected payloads locally.

## Checked In
- Encyclopedia shell, curated chapters, schemas, public payload-free manifests, tools, validation logic, and source-generation code.

## User Provided
- EarthBound ROM file and optional local decomp/source workspace paths.

## Generated Locally
- Byte-equivalent `src/`, local `asset-manifests/`, renderer fixtures, source snapshots, search catalogs, extracted references, preview sheets, SPC/WAV exports, and cache files.

## Never Distributed
- ROM bytes, raw extracted copyrighted assets, generated audio/images that contain ROM-derived content, or generated byte-equivalent source built from the user's ROM.

## Release Shape
- The packaged app should be usable in authored mode without a ROM.
- Selecting a ROM should verify size and SHA-1, then generate local workspace artifacts under an app-data folder.
- Entries should keep provenance visible: project-authored, generated locally, ROM-derived local, or reference/imported.
- Run `npm run audit:release` before packaging.

entries.title: Release Readiness Checklist
entries.summary: Current release blockers and presentation gaps before publishing the standalone Electron app.
entries.body:
This checklist keeps the release target visible inside the authored app.

## Package Boundary
- Authored release builds must contain no ROM, source files, generated source entries, asset entries, raw extracted payloads, preview sheets, SPC/WAV exports, or cache files.
- The app package contains documentation, learning paths, ROM-knowledge chapters, source-safe workflow pages, and the first-run local workspace shell.
- ROM-backed source, graphics, maps, audio, table manifests, and ZIP exports are generated only under the user's app-data workspace after ROM verification.

## Binary Release Work
- Windows unsigned NSIS and ZIP artifacts can be produced from this workspace.
- Linux ZIP artifacts can be produced from this Windows workspace.
- Linux AppImage should be built on Linux/CI or on Windows with symlink privileges enabled.
- A real app icon, publisher metadata, project license, and third-party notice bundle are still required before a public binary release.

## Generator Work
- Current Electron generator stages create local workspace manifests, source scaffolds, ROM/header/bank manifests, and family handoff manifests.
- Full renderer stages still need to attach compiled sprites, palette-applied sheets, map previews, SPC exports, WAV exports, and searchable generated catalog hydration.

## Content And Access Gaps
- NPC AI bytes, concrete shop selector paths, encoded PSI menu row decoding, map preview/editor rules, audio runtime state capture, and asset-family editor rules remain the highest-value content polish targets.
- The Asset Library is the correct home for generated content, but it needs per-family browsers once the generator outputs real rendered artifacts.
- The Local Workspace and Release Artifact Policy pages should remain the clearest explanation of project-authored versus ROM-derived local material.

## Detection

## Policy
- The encyclopedia should use the ROM to verify and regenerate local manifests, source maps, and metadata.
- It should not commit generated copyrighted asset payloads into the repo by default.
- ROM-derived outputs should live under ignored build folders unless a specific source-safe artifact is intentionally promoted.

## Next Implementation Hook
A future `build:from-rom` command can run validation and extraction tools when this page reports a matching ROM, then refresh the generated encyclopedia catalog.

entries.title: Semantic Frontiers
entries.summary: The next work after scaffold closure: semantics, contracts, fixtures, and editable assets.
entries.body:
### Source and runtime semantics

- `C0`: overworld/entity/task/movement/runtime contracts.
- `C1`: text engine, CCS leaves, menus, battle front ends, file select.
- `C2`: battle runtime, action dispatch, status/effect families, battle visuals.
- `C4`: renderer, text tiles, HDMA/color/window helpers, movement presentation.
- `EF`: save/SRAM, debug/menu routines, reusable late helpers, and text/data tails.

### Data-contract splitters

- `D5`, `CF`, `D0`, and `D8`: complete as first table splitters; remaining work is subrecord semantics and source/data emission.
- `D7`, `DA`, `DC`, `DF`, `E0`, `E1`: smaller inferred table/pointer contract promotions.

### Script, text, and VM assets

- `C3`: source/data split is mapped; improve event/actionscript opcode semantics, operand names, and callback contracts.
- `C5..C9`: text-script export and text command decoder regression corpus.
- `EF`: split large help/battle/menu text run using D5/C1 consumers.

### Raw asset emission

- `CA..CE`: battle background, battle sprite, animation, PSI, swirl, and Sound Stone assets.
- `D1..D4`: full-bank overworld sprite graphics slabs.
- `D6..DF`: map tile, arrangement, graphics, palette, and audio payloads.
- `E2..EE`: audio-pack banks; `EE` needs an explicit padding/tail policy.

## Chapter Status
- Maturity: `draft-narrative`
- Scope: `ROM knowledge`
- Scope meaning: Facts about EarthBound's original data, routines, runtime behavior, or asset contracts.
- Source root: `authored-release-baseline`
- Primary evidence notes: 12
- Additional related notes: 4
## Contract Model
An asset/data contract is the evidence-backed boundary between original ROM bytes and editor or port work. It does not contain the copyrighted payload. It records what owns the bytes, how those bytes are located, what decoder or renderer shape is expected, and how a local user can regenerate or verify the derived output from their own ROM.
That makes contracts different from raw extraction. A raw `.gfx`, `.pal`, `.arr`, BRR sample, collision table, or object bundle can be extracted locally, but the checked-in source-safe object is the recipe: stable ID, bank/range, size, hash, decoder class, dependencies, uncertainty, and validation command. Those recipes are the durable knowledge layer.
## The Four Layers
- ROM recipe layer: records the source span, expected byte count, expected SHA-1, compression, and table or pointer evidence.
- Portable asset layer: describes ignored local outputs such as raw slices, decompressed bytes, preview PNGs, palette JSON, object bundles, scene contracts, or audio intermediates.
- Semantic ID layer: gives tools stable names such as battle background IDs, sprite group IDs, map object IDs, map tileset IDs, and table-contract names so consumers do not depend on bare SNES addresses.
- Validation layer: proves the recipe against a user-supplied ROM and records which generated reports or hashes make the contract reproducible.
## Current Coverage
The manifest pipeline now covers every currently mapped asset/data bank from `CA` through `EE`, plus the hand-curated EF debug seed manifest. The latest local status reports `38` manifests, `2218` assets, and `6174` output recipes. The output recipes include raw ROM-backed outputs, LZHAL decompression, palette JSON and swatches, battle-background previews, battle-sprite previews, default-palette overworld sprite sheets, and composed battle-background and battle-sprite PNGs.
This does not make every asset family semantically final. It gives the project a repeatable source-safe inventory. Interpretation remains a separate layer: which assets belong together, which runtime tables choose them, what renderer assumptions are proven, and which editor fields have evidence.
## Major Families
- `CA..CE`: battle backgrounds, battle sprites, palettes, arrangements, animation visuals, and related compressed graphics.
- `D1..D5`: overworld sprite payloads, later joined through sprite group, frame, animation-role, map placement, and object bundle contracts.
- `CF..D0`, `D5`, `D8`, `DA`, `DE`, `DF`, and `EF`: map doors, placements, battle/menu tables, collision records, map palettes, tile animation graphics, upload scripts, and pointer tables.
- `E0..E1`: UI, font, town map, intro/title/ending/cast, and presentation assets.
- `E2..EE`: audio-pack payloads, now promoted from bank-level coverage into `LOAD_SPC700_DATA` stream contracts, track-to-pack snapshot rules, and a renderer/backend boundary.
## Editing Rules
The safe editing unit is the highest contract that already preserves the dependency chain. For a single compressed battle-background graphic, the useful edit boundary includes its graphics payload, matching palette, arrangement, preview renderer, and manifest hash. For an overworld NPC, the useful edit boundary is not just a D1-D5 `.gfx` payload; it includes sprite group identity, runtime slot records, animation role, map placement, movement/script target, event flag, and text pointer context.
A generated preview is evidence that a decoder path is plausible. It is not by itself an authoring schema. A family reaches editable status only when the contract explains stable fields, runtime-selected values, and which local outputs are disposable rebuild products.
- Keep ROM-derived payloads in ignored build/cache paths.
- Commit manifests, tools, contracts, summaries, and validation reports only when they are payload-free.
- Use semantic IDs in editor and port work; keep raw bank addresses as provenance and compatibility anchors.
- Treat palette, arrangement, collision, OAM, and script dependencies as part of an asset's contract when the runtime consumes them together.
- Do not rename a generated asset family as semantically final until the relevant runtime selector or table has been followed.
## Confidence Boundary
The current asset pipeline is strong at inventory, extraction, and many visual preview paths. It is strongest where runtime contracts have been joined: map objects, sprite roles, collision pointer/runtime bits, palette pointer tables, tile animation upload records, and many battle visual assets.
The main weak spots are the places where a payload is mapped but the consumer-side authoring meaning is still thin: some map collision low bits, DA palette metadata words, text/common palette preview joining, palette-settings-only tilesets, event/actionscript behavior semantics, and the distinction between ROM audio facts and local playback/export tooling. Those limits belong in the visible contract layer rather than hidden in generated pages.

## Chapter Status
- Maturity: `draft-narrative`
- Scope: `ROM knowledge`
- Scope meaning: Facts about EarthBound's original data, routines, runtime behavior, or asset contracts.
- Source root: `authored-release-baseline`
- Primary evidence notes: 16
## Current Boundary
The audio banks now have a payload-free contract layer for `169` audio packs, `192` music tracks, and `169` pack pointer entries. Every represented pack parses as an `ok` `LOAD_SPC700_DATA` stream, and the track table resolves to the primary, secondary, and sequence pack order used by `CHANGE_MUSIC`.
The ROM-facing facts are the source ranges, byte counts, SHA-1 hashes, stream block transcripts, pack selector evidence, and track mappings. ROM-derived payload bytes, APU RAM images, SPC snapshots, and WAV renders are generated locally from a user's ROM and stay out of the checked-in encyclopedia.
## What Is Now Teachable
- Banks `E2..EE` are overwhelmingly source-order audio-pack payloads, with E6's custom `AUDIO_PACK_1` handled as a special inline block instead of being double-counted.
- Audio packs are modeled as loader streams, not opaque blobs: each stream has one or more destination blocks and a terminating loader handshake.
- Music tracks can be described as pack recipes: primary sample pack, secondary sample pack, and sequence pack, with unchanged or `$FF` entries skipped by the runtime.
- The local corpus tooling can rebuild deterministic APU RAM and later SPC/WAV evidence for selected tracks, but those outputs are local ROM-derived artifacts rather than checked-in ROM documentation.
- Generated audio outputs belong under ignored `build/audio` paths. The committed encyclopedia contains contracts, not mirrored audio payload bytes.
## ROM And Tooling Boundary
The pack contracts describe the ROM's loadable music payloads. Backend work describes how our tools replay those payloads through emulation, capture state, and render WAVs.
Keep those layers separate when reading the encyclopedia: `LOAD_SPC700_DATA`, pack pointers, track recipes, and `CHANGE_MUSIC` behavior are ROM knowledge; ares harnesses, libgme renders, result summaries, and playback/export manifests are project tooling evidence.

## Chapter Status
- Maturity: `draft-narrative`
- Scope: `ROM knowledge`
- Scope meaning: Facts about EarthBound's original data, routines, runtime behavior, or asset contracts.
- Source root: `authored-release-baseline`

## Stream Model
The runtime owner for this contract is `C0:AB06 LoadSpc700DataStream`. The loader waits for the SPC ready signature on the APU ports, temporarily disables NMI while it streams data, writes block payloads to APU destinations, and exits through the loader's final handshake.
The portable contract is intentionally simpler than the SNES routine. Each audio pack is represented as a sequence of blocks: a `u16 payload_byte_count`, then a `u16 apu_destination` plus payload bytes when the count is nonzero. A zero count terminates the stream and records the `$0500` terminal handshake behavior.
## Coverage
- `169` audio packs are represented.
- `169` pack pointer entries are represented.
- All represented streams currently parse with status `ok`.
- Every known audio pack has a byte-exact ROM source range and SHA-1.
- The track table currently has `0` unused pack IDs.
- E6's custom `AUDIO_PACK_1` block is represented as a custom inline audio pack instead of a normal source-order insert.
## Bank Run Boundary
The source-order run covers the heavy `E2..EE` audio banks, with the large `EE:9201..EE:FFFF` tail still called out as a separate unexplained slack region. The bank maps prove source readiness for the opaque payloads, while this stream contract proves that the payloads can be replayed through the same loader shape the game uses.
Pack identity is not the same thing as internal audio meaning. The pack contract says where bytes come from, how they load, how they validate, and which tracks select them. BRR sample names, sequence commands, and instrument semantics need their own evidence before they become ROM-facing facts.
## Editing Rule
The safe stream-editing unit is a complete pack transcript. Changing a payload byte, destination, or block count without updating range/hash validation and track ownership desynchronizes the loader contract from the source ROM evidence.
Audio packs are validated load streams at this layer. Sample and sequence authoring is a later layer that consumes this contract instead of replacing it.

## Chapter Status
- Maturity: `draft-narrative`
- Scope: `Local generated evidence`
- Scope meaning: Evidence produced locally from a user ROM or decomp workspace and kept out of distributed builds.
- Source root: `authored-release-baseline`
- Primary evidence notes: 3
- Additional related notes: 13
## What The Seed Contains
The APU RAM seed contains the 64 KiB memory image after the relevant `LOAD_SPC700_DATA` streams have been applied in runtime order. It proves that the pack stream contracts and track mapping can construct deterministic memory images.
A seed is not a running SPC state. It records loaded memory and the post-load track-command requirement, but it does not by itself prove the registers, DSP state, timers, mailbox timing, or rendered audio.
## Missing Runtime State
- SPC700 CPU registers are not captured.
- DSP registers are not captured.
- APU control and timer state are not captured.
- APUIO mailbox state is only partially modeled.
- Driver elapsed cycles and post-command timing are not captured.
## Renderer Gates
- `diagnostic_apu_ram_seed` is open and useful today.
- `complete_spc_snapshot` requires runtime state capture or emulation evidence.
- `local_pcm_wav_export` is tooling evidence: it requires a renderer backend, output hashes, and render metrics.
- `snes_spc` is a lightweight renderer lane once a suitable SPC snapshot exists.
- `ares` is the accuracy-first lane for proving command delivery, runtime state, and capture timing.
## Editing Rule
A built APU RAM image is loaded-memory evidence. A playable/exportable artifact also needs a runtime-state source, backend identity, timing basis, output hashes, and render metrics.
A renderer entry must identify whether it is describing ROM behavior or project tooling. Registers, DSP state, timers, command byte, timing basis, and backend version are tooling evidence unless they are tied directly back to ROM execution.

## Track Load Order
`CHANGE_MUSIC` gives the snapshot contract its order. A track resolves to primary sample pack, secondary sample pack, and sequence pack. The runtime loads changed packs in that order, skips unchanged entries, skips `$FF`, updates `CURRENT_MUSIC_TRACK`, and finally writes the one-based track index to `APUPort0` through `C0:ABBD`.
Cold start adds one more rule: `C4:FB58 InitializeMusicSubsystem` loads the row-0 sequence/common pack before ordinary track changes. A snapshot builder that omits that bootstrap can still load pack bytes, but it is not modeling the same runtime state.
## Diagnostic APU RAM Seed
- The snapshot corpus can construct a 64 KiB APU RAM image after replaying the selected pack streams.
- The seed is ROM-derived and must remain an ignored local diagnostic artifact.
- The seed records the post-load track command requirement, but it does not execute the APU driver after writing the command byte.
- Renderer fixtures should point to ignored seed files and pack transcripts instead of embedding ROM-derived bytes in committed JSON.
- The useful status label for this stage is `diagnostic_apu_ram_seed`, not `complete_spc_snapshot`.
## Tooling Contract
The generated tooling path has distinct jobs: build and validate audio pack contracts, inspect track-to-pack mappings, build selected track snapshots, build an ignored corpus, and create renderer fixtures. Those jobs are not the renderer.
Track snapshot entries describe which packs a track uses and what memory image can be reconstructed. Playback and export evidence belongs to the backend/tooling layer.
## Editing Rule
A track edit starts as a change to the track's pack recipe. Changing a sequence pack, sample pack, or common bootstrap assumption requires rebuilding the snapshot corpus and comparing the pack transcript before playback/export results are trusted.

## Chapter Status
- Maturity: `draft-narrative`

## D5 Gameplay Spine
D5 now has a practical gameplay-table spine. The split plan reconciles the post-pad region exactly and identifies the source-order families that matter for battle, items, shops, teleport, phone, growth, map destinations, timed delivery, initial stats, and enemies.
For battle editing, three D5 families are the current anchors: the battle action descriptor table at `D5:7B68`, the battle PSI ability table at `D5:8A50`, and the enemy configuration table at `D5:9589`.
## Action Rows
The `D5:7B68` action table is no longer merely battle-action-like. The strongest current read is a 12-byte row: direction, target, action type, PP or cost byte, message pointer, and action handler pointer. Early entries line up cleanly with no-effect, bash, shoot, spy, pray, and the PSI quartet runs.
The confidence is strongest where table metadata, reference layout, local wrapper quartets, shared helper signatures, and C2 action bodies all agree. Later rows now have status, stat/resource, physical/special, and flavor-tail anchors, but the table should still label tail outliers and reference-assisted names honestly.
## Battle Action Confidence
The early table is the cleanest slice: PSI Rockin, Fire, Freeze, and Thunder rows line up by direction, target, type, cost, message pointer, and C2 handler pointer. Later rows have improved local anchors too: status-action bodies, stat/resource mutation bodies, physical/special wrappers, and flavor-tail no-op rows.
That gives the editor model a tiered confidence map. Early action rows can be presented with strong names and fields. Later rows should show their current local body evidence, but keep reference-assisted names and unresolved tail outliers visibly qualified.
- Strong: row stride, first four metadata bytes, message pointer, handler pointer, early PSI quartets, and several late C2 body families.
- Medium: reference-backed row names where local handler behavior is compatible but not fully followed end to end.
- Open: tail entries whose table position is clear but whose gameplay role is still presentation-heavy or caller-thin.
## Enemy Rows
`D5:9589` is the strongest current local crosswalk to the enemy configuration table. The record stride is `0x5E`, local text extraction from `D5:9589 + 1 + n * 0x5E` yields enemy names, and local code reaches the family through a selector with stride `#$005E`.
The safest field names are the ones backed by both local consumers and the reference struct shape: article flag, enemy name, encounter text pointer, death text pointer, music, final action, final action argument, row, max-called behavior, and mirror success. These rows are not just stats; they connect battle presentation, text, audio, and action selection.
## Cross Table Joins
The most useful battle model is not a single table. Enemy rows can select final actions, action rows point at text and handlers, PSI ability rows point back into action rows, and C1/C2/C3 helpers turn those fields into menu choices, target prompts, row formatting, and battle text.
That is the reason battle and enemy chapters should be read with the PSI/menu chapter rather than as a competing explanation. `D5:7B68`, `D5:8A50`, and `D5:9589` are separate storage families, but the runtime presents them as one battle-facing authoring surface.
## Editing Rule
A battle table edit should follow the row to its consumers before making a name stronger. If a field points at EF text, C2 action code, C1 menu text, or C3 formatting helpers, that downstream behavior is part of the contract.
The table is joined data: enemy row, selected action row, action message pointer, action handler pointer, PSI ability row when applicable, and battle visual/text neighbors. Raw D5 offsets are provenance, not the primary authoring model.

## Chapter Status
- Maturity: `draft-narrative`
- Scope: `ROM knowledge`
- Scope meaning: Facts about EarthBound's original data, routines, runtime behavior, or asset contracts.
- Source root: `authored-release-baseline`
- Primary evidence notes: 11
- Additional related notes: 5
## System Shape
Battle visuals are not a single asset type. They are a family of compressed graphics, palettes, arrangements, size metadata, token tables, runtime palette effects, and renderer staging code. The source-safe contract should keep those pieces linkable even when the decoded PNG preview is only a local build artifact.
The current manifest pipeline can extract and preview palette-aware battle backgrounds and battle sprites. For battle backgrounds, matching graphics, palette, and arrangement payloads can produce composed arrangement previews. For battle sprites, observed enemy-table sprite/palette combinations can produce size-aware composed previews.
## What Is Proven
- `CA..CE` asset maps provide bank ownership, labels, payload filenames, CPU spans, file offsets, sizes, and first-byte fingerprints for battle visual payloads.
- The extraction pipeline records raw and LZHAL-decompressed outputs, palette-aware tile previews, battle-background arrangement previews, and battle-sprite composed previews.
- C2 notes cover battle background loading, palette effects, battle sprite rendering, and palette-tail behavior.
- C3 notes expose battle visual token, offset, and palette table evidence, giving the visual byte payloads runtime selector context.
- C4 notes cover visual frame copy and footprint tables, which matters for how visual data reaches presentation memory.
## Authoring Boundary
A battle background edit is safe only when the graphics, palette, arrangement, compression, and preview path remain coherent. A battle sprite edit also needs size and palette pairing evidence from the observed enemy table path. The editor-facing unit should be a composed contract, not a single decompressed byte stream.
Generated names like `BATTLE_BACKGROUND_GFX_86` or `BATTLE_BACKGROUND_ARR_43` are stable handles for tooling, but the display-facing meaning should come from runtime use, enemy/table context, and rendered previews rather than from the numeric suffix alone.
## Known Limits
- Preview coverage is strong for observed combinations, but not every possible runtime composition is necessarily a designed authoring combination.
- Palette effects and battle visual tokens should be described through C2/C3 runtime evidence before editor UI treats them as intuitive art controls.
- The manifest layer preserves payload provenance; final battle-effect semantics still need curated pages for major effect families.

entries.body:
## Chapter Status
- Maturity: `draft-narrative`
- Scope: `ROM knowledge`
- Scope meaning: Facts about EarthBound's original data, routines, runtime behavior, or asset contracts.
- Source root: `authored-release-baseline`
- Primary evidence notes: 8
- Additional related notes: 8
## Template Model
Many C3 scripts are better read as templates than as one-off scene scripts. They install a callback, start a recurring animation task, seed a few script variables, wait on a native predicate, and then release or hand off the current visual entity.
The key values in these templates are often animation IDs, `V0` or `V4` gates, wait timers, random-choice lists, target coordinates, and release-tail addresses. Their meaning depends on the template, not on a global enum.
## Temporary Actor Family
The temporary actor movement notes split several useful families: timed-delivery cleanup pulses, `C4:0015`-gated pulse-and-release loops, a `V0`-selected animation phase loop, random wandering setup, NPC attention or neighbor-cache loops, and shared current-entity release tails.
For example, `C3:A3B7` clears `V4`, classifies the current slot against area bounds, chooses a cardinal direction or adjusts the current direction, installs the direction through C0 helpers, derives a movement timer, then chooses a random wait from `30,60,90,120` before looping.
## V0 And V4
`V4` is a strong local gate in movement pulse families: some loops only show animation `1` while `V4` is true, or count down before restoring animation `0`. `V0` appears as an animation phase selector in temporary actor and attention paths, where several short cases choose different pulse/wait shapes.
Those are family-local meanings. `V0` and `V4` are script variables with known roles in specific templates, not universal variable names across all of C3.
## Editing Rule
A template editor should show the whole shape: installed callbacks, started tasks, animation IDs, script variables, wait timers, random lists, native predicates, and release tail. Editing just the animation byte without the task and predicate context is too narrow.
Animation IDs `0`, `1`, and `FF` are common in these templates, but their authoring meaning should stay tied to the visual-profile helpers and script family that use them. Repetition alone is not enough to make a global animation enum.

## Chapter Status
- Maturity: `draft-narrative`
- Scope: `ROM knowledge`
- Scope meaning: Facts about EarthBound's original data, routines, runtime behavior, or asset contracts.
- Source root: `authored-release-baseline`
- Primary evidence notes: 6
- Additional related notes: 10
## Operand Boundary
The C3 decoder now knows enough about callback byte shapes to be useful: it distinguishes bank-local short calls from low-word callback installers, prints named callback targets, labels common operands such as frames, script variables, animation IDs, and event-flag words, and keeps raw bytes visible on every decoded line.
That is a readability layer, not a license to name every literal. Inline arguments become semantics only when the target callback, local script family, or downstream runtime helper proves what the value controls.
## Two Argument Classes
`EVENT_CALLROUTINE` arguments are consumed immediately by the native helper and usually belong to that helper's contract. Callback installer operands are different: opcodes such as `EVENT_SET_POSITION_CHANGE_CALLBACK` and `EVENT_SET_PHYSICS_CALLBACK` store low-word targets that bind long-lived C0 or C4 behavior to the active entity.
The earlier decoder bug is a good warning sign. Callback installers looked like C3-local pointers until the binding correction proved they commonly point back to C0 callback routines. The durable lesson is that operand shape is not the same as operand meaning.
## Current Strong Labels
- Mutation operation bytes can use the C0 interpreter names `AND`, `OR`, `ADD`, and `EOR` because the interpreter table proves them.
- Event flag words can be labeled where the callback argument schema already ties them to flag checks.
- Velocity and relative-position words can show signed decimal meaning beside raw hex values.
- `$5D9A` can be called a queue-pending or transient special-state flag where the C0/EF queue notes support that read.
- Callback pointers for movement, projection, velocity integration, passive no-op behavior, and screen-position callbacks can use their C0/C4 names once the installer opcode class is known.
## Editing Rule
A C3 editor should show raw operand bytes, friendly labels, and evidence level together. Strong labels can become controls. Medium labels should stay descriptive. Weak labels should remain literal until a local family note or native callback contract proves the field.
The safest UI is not a screen full of raw hex or a screen full of overconfident names. It is a joined view: opcode, operand bytes, target helper, known argument schema, installed callback lifetime, and the notes that prove the interpretation.
